records.text: Exploring New Growth Engines Two major sectors of the Chinese economy have undergone significant changes in recent years. In trade, China’s share of total US imports has dropped sharply following two US-China trade wars, reaching levels last seen before China joined the WTO in 2001 (left panel of Exhibit 1). In the property market, new housing starts have fallen significantly since the government mandated property developers to deleverage in late 2020, reversing nearly all the gains made since the housing reform of 1998 (right panel of Exhibit 1). With exports to the US limited by tariffs and the property market now a much smaller part of the economy, policymakers face the challenge of finding new engines of growth in the coming years. So far, Chinese exporters have successfully diversified their destinations away from the US and maintained overall export growth. Admittedly, some of the products destined for the US were rerouted through ASEAN after US tariff increases and reached the US indirectly. From a fundamental point of view, China’s strong manufacturing competitiveness, combined with an undervalued currency, has led to significant increases in China’s share of many other countries’ imports, especially among emerging markets. In addition to final products, exports of intermediate and capital goods have also risen notably as Chinese manufacturers expand globally and build factories abroad. Real disposable income growth has slid to 0%Y in 3Q, but the savings rate has ticked down. The flow of savings, per Money and Credit data, likely rose anew in October and November, with strong consumer credit flows aiding, we think, durable goods purchases – a bright spot in expenditure data. Business loans growth is firm, per Money and Credit data, and this chimes with robust business capex in 2025. We see some slowdown over 2026, but see balanced risks to our forecasts. In this note, we summarise the latest growth indicators (see Economics: Chart Gallery ). What next: Most market participants we talk to now expect growth to tick up in 1Q, if for no other reason than the ONS' apparent challenges with properly seasonally adjusting 1H growth data. While we have long cautioned about this issue, we think it largely stems from nominal and inflation data over 1H in recent years. If inflationary pressures are not as severe in 1H26, perhaps the "residual seasonality effect" will not be as meaningful this year as it was in 2023, 2024 and 2025. In 2025, in any case, the effect was amplified by US tariffs-related front-loading in activity. That said, we take the initial market reaction with a pinch of salt, not least because of the risk that President Trump intensifies pressure on other economies such as Iran or Russia. Temporary fall in oil prices unlikely to shift policy: We think central banks will generally take a ‘look through’ approach to the change in oil prices stemming from Venezuela. Indeed, as ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane recently argued, “a supply shock to the relative price level of energy does not pose the same risk to medium-term inflation as a shock to domestic demand”. As a result, a temporary fall (or rise) in energy prices that is also accompanied by a positive (negative) GDP impact does not necessarily justify a monetary policy response. That said, scenarios which push oil prices meaningfully lower could nonetheless shift central banks in a slightly more dovish direction. For example, in the scenario of a strong increase in supply, lower oil prices would reduce the ‘tension’ between the two aspects of the Fed’s mandate and give it even more free rein to support the labour market. A new and potentially more dovishly inclined Fed chair could use this as ammunition to push for further easing. We think the bar for the ECB may be somewhat higher still. After imposing a 50% principal haircut, Venezuela could potentially offer investors a 20yr ‘new bond’ with a 4.4% coupon and a 10yr zero coupon bond for the PDI. Even so, for much of 2025, we fielded numerous investor questions about whether Nestle's FCF would even cover its c. CHF8bn annual dividend payment. After a weak FCF performance in H1-25, the good news is that Nestlé has guided FY25 FCF to be above CHF8bn, which will fully cover its dividend payment, but of course the market will want to see evidence because the FY25 FCF guidance of at least CHF8bn implies its H2-25 FCF will be at least CHF5.7bn, almost 3x the level of the FCF delivered in H1-25. Nestlé has also said that the step up in FCF in H2-25 will exclude a CHF2.1bn dividend from Froneri (Nestle's ice cream JV with PAI), which will help reduce net debt, but will not be a benefit to its FCF. Although Nestle has indicated that it is looking to exit its Waters division, Blue Bottle Coffee and half its VMS business, none of these transactions had been executed before year-end, so will not benefit FCF or debt reduction in 2025, but should potentially help in 2026. 5 January 2026 81 Barclays | Global Consumer Staples

The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

These are both within the range of “normal” increases over the last year, although, if anything, with primary rents a bit on the softer side. But we continue to see the 13bp increase in OER in September (which is free of measurement issues) as possibly the start of more sustained slowing in shelter inflation. records.text: Euro Area Outlook 2026: Cyclical Boost, Structural Drag, Unchanged Rates We expect 2026 to be a better year for the Euro area economy than 2025 on the back of the German fiscal expansion, reduced global tariff tensions and resilient consumer spending. That said, we only look for a small growth improvement as Europe faces notable structural drags from Chinese export competition and weak potential growth. As a result, we forecast Euro area growth of 1.4% on a Q4/Q4 basis this year, up slightly from last year’s pace of 1.3%, but broadly similar to the consensus. We see three main reasons for a cyclical pickup this year. First, we look for more fiscal support, driven primarily by Germany (Exhibit 2). We believe that the German fiscal expansion remains on track, as most of the pickup in spending is in defence, social spending and subsidies (instead of infrastructure investment, which is at higher risk of under-delivery). Assuming that the plan has already been activated internally, the CEO might talk about a c.18 months time frame when he speaks in the spring 2026. To reach this margin level, we believe Kering would likely need to grow at c.10% organic growth in the next few years. Under this "bull case" we foresee Kering reaching a terminal EBIT margin of 25%, which the company was able to achieve in the past. Our Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) is now at c.0.85 and has rebounded since ‘Liberation day’, with both RAI PC1 (‘Growth optimism’) and RAI PC2 (‘Monetary policy optimism’) supporting the recovery. In Q4, a weak labour market drove a new high in RAI PC2 due to expectations of a ‘central bank put’. However, into 2026, markets faded expectations for central bank easing and risk appetite has been increasingly driven by better growth expectations (RAI PC1 is at the upper end of its range, RAI PC2 has declined). We would expect growth to remain the key driver of risk appetite in 2026, especially with better growth in 1H 2026, and RAI PC1 and PC2 to move more opposite to each other. However, we do not think that RAI PC2 will become a sustained drag due to our benign inflation view globally and a weak labour market supporting further Fed cuts. Equity/bond correlations should be more negative but the bond buffer for equities is limited and risk of negative rate shocks remains. records.text: Although fiscal policy remains contractionary in the rest of Europe, we expect defence spending to pick up across the Euro area. The additional defence expenditure is part of multiannual European initiative, likely to deliver a notable growth impulse and will be facilitated by common issuance of EU debt in the second half of 2026. As a result, we look for a neutral area-wide fiscal impulse in 2026, a sharp improvement from prior years (Exhibit 3). Second, we expect the headwinds from the global trade tensions to diminish this year (Exhibit 4). Our analysis points to an area-wide real GDP level hit of 0.4% from the rise in tariffs and the associated uncertainty. EU exports to the US have dropped sharply, but demand in other export destinations has held up better. This supports our view that the tariff-related growth drag has likely peaked and will fade into 2026. A restructuring could enhance creditor recovery while preserving near- term liquidity by pairing a new base bond with a Value Recovery Instrument (VRI) or offering a Macro-linked Bond. The IMF has increasingly supported state- contingent features in high-volatility cases: Sri Lanka’s proposed Macro-Linked Bonds adjust coupons to nominal GDP performance (See: Sri Lanka Economics & Strategy: The Final Stretch of Debt Restructuring); Zambia introduced commodity- linked triggers tied to copper revenues; and Suriname adopted macro step-ups linked to external solvency improvements. Common across these cases is that upside is back-loaded and only realized if the sovereign’s capacity to pay improves. For Venezuela, a similar approach could link payouts to net oil export receipts or government oil take, verified by independent reporting. This structure preserves stabilization space early in the program while offering conditional upside to investors. records.text: A gradual slowdown in long-term growth with shifting drivers China’s GDP growth has decelerated meaningfully since the 2008 GFC, to around 5% per year in recent years from around 10% during the 2000s. To investigate the driving forces of the long-term growth slowdown, we decompose GDP growth into contributions from labor, human capital, physical capital and total factor productivity (TFP), based on the production function accounting framework (Exhibit 23). Physical capital used to be the main driver of growth during 2009-2020, fueled by multiple large stimulus cycles, while its contribution started to moderate in recent years on the back of already elevated government debt levels and falling return on capital. Labor has started to slightly hold back growth since mid-2010s after working-age population peaked in China and is expected to decline in the coming decades, though human capital accumulation may provide a partial offset. TFP growth slowed meaningfully post the GFC as China prioritized infrastructure and property investments, but it has shown modest improvement in recent years thanks to the rapid growth of high-tech manufacturing sectors. As China’s economy faces a shrinking working-age population and investment share of GDP has been consistently above 40% over the past two decades, the outlook for long-term GDP growth will largely depend on TFP . High-tech and strategic areas, urban renewal, and infrastructure related to people’s livelihood are likely target investment areas. Even with strong determination and sufficient resources, transforming China’s economy into one driven by consumption and services will take years. With a more reluctant, measured approach, it could take decades. Signals from the 15th Five-Year Plan proposal approved at the 4th Plenum in late October support our view. With “building a modern industrial system” and “accelerating high-tech self-reliance” topping the priority list, Chinese exports and current account are likely to stay strong in the coming years. Industry store count increased 7% from 2019-2025, a significant acceleration vs 4% in the prior five years. During that period, sales also grew meaningfully, effectively supporting that capacity growth. But more recently, industry store count has declined q/q through 2025 and is set to go negative y/y. We are seeing the biggest decline in drug stores, and modest declines among specialty food stores and slower growth of supermarkets, convenience stores and pet supply stores, while select channels are still growing (club, dollar stores). Why is that capacity an issue now? Sales growth has moderated, the consumer seems to be under more pressure and is shifting to value channels, and delivery is accelerating. records.text: Goldilocks re-cycling - capturing new tailwinds, managing old headwinds (1) Modest growth pick-up supported by fiscal policy, easing inflation Our macro baseline remains friendly given sturdy global growth, helped by more policy easing, and falling inflation. Our economists expect above-consensus global GDP growth of 2.8% with core inflation declining to 2.1% by YE2026 – growth is expected to be stronger in 1H. Our US business cycle scores are expected to improve with a small pick-up in our growth score but easier policy and falling inflation (Exhibit 5). But while we expect a continued ‘Goldilocks’ backdrop in 2026, drivers are different to 2025. Last year, growth optimism was boosted by AI capex while Fed expectations shifted dovish due to a weak labour market. This year, we would expect growth to take over from rates relief and more broadening of procyclical impulses, helped by fiscal easing in the US, Germany and Japan. However, despite good growth, we expect labour markets to remain somewhat weaker, in part due to AI adoption and productivity focus. Our economists expect the global growth/inflation mix to improve and are most optimistic on growth in the US and China (Exhibit 6). Our economists expect above-consensus US GDP growth of 2.8% in 2026, a pick-up from 2.2% in 2025, boosted by the Big Beautiful Bill in 1H 2026. They also expect falling inflation due to a fading tariff impacts, weak housing and labour markets, as well as falling oil prices. In addition, they rema

ediate and capital goods have also risen notably as Chinese manufacturers expand globally and build factories abroad. We expect this trend to continue, with export volumes rising 5-6% per year over the next few years. As a result, exports to non-US countries are likely to remain a significant driver of China’s economic growth. In contrast, the government’s effort to restructure the domestic economy from property and infrastructure-driven to consumption and services-driven is still in its early stages. In 2026, private consumption will continue to be weighed down by a weak labor market and falling house prices, making higher government consumption the only option to stabilize overall consumption growth (Exhibit 2). records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 208/01/2026 Oil market impact: The uncertainty for Venezuelan oil flows comes on top of an already bearish oil market. We believe supply volumes can increase, which would push crude prices further down, only if sanctions are lifted – until then supply risks are skewed upwards, in our view. If and when sanctions are lifted, however, we anticipate significant price weakness for a few months as a significant amount of floating barrels unload, until new supply risks emerge. Further out, we foresee a gradual recovery of production and anticipate the market to overestimate the size and speed of recovery at that time. US pressure has hit Venezuelan exports: Venezuela’s state-owned oil and gas company PDVSA exported roughly 750kbd in recent months (down from ~1.1mbd earlier in 2025), with about 400kbd bound for Chinese independent teapot refiners as state-owned firms shun these barrels due to sanction concerns. The US has taken around 17% (~125kbd) in 2025 – down from 35% in 2024 following changes to Chevron’s licence – while the remaining cargoes are shipped to Cuba and a handful of other destinations such as Spain and Italy under the previous licences. Venezuelan supply has been under severe pressure from US sanctions and shipping blockades (see Figure 1). records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 05 January 2026 Citi Research 8 We continue to like the Venezuela bonds. We have been advocating going long Venezuela bonds since Feb 2024. Recently we have increased our overweight position (Venezuela Emerging Markets Strategy - Going All-in: Assessing the potential bond prices’ upside). The removal of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro is constructive for bonds, even if the Chavismo ideology survives in a modified form. Base case: +3–5 point rally on Monday. Bonds already reflect optimism, but still have room to grind higher since they are trading well below our estimate of recovery value (high 40s see below), in our view. A complex restructuring in the making. We expect Venezuela’s debt restructuring to be exceptionally complex—arguably comparable to Greece’s 2012 PSI—given the sheer size of the liability stock, the highly fragmented creditor base (sovereign bonds, bilateral creditors, and arbitration/judgment claims), and the overlay of US sanctions and ongoing asset-attachment litigation. Unlike more recent CAC- driven restructurings (e.g., Ecuador or Argentina), a Venezuelan process will likely require a multi-track, multi-year settlement framework, with outcomes highly sensitive to assumptions around post-transition GDP normalization and the pace of oil-production recovery. records.text: 8 January 2026 US Economic Perspectives Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 3 What might a productivity boom mean for monetary policy? In the near -term at least, the most important consideration is whether productivity gains, perhaps driven by AI, allow firms to continue to substitute away from labor, leaving the labor market in a precarious state. Our baseline remains that the labor market will stabilize this year, supported by a stronger growth outlook as headwinds fade (e.g., trade policy uncertainty) and tailwinds emerge (e.g., greater fiscal support from tax cuts). But weaker labor market outcomes remain a clear risk. More generally, we expect continued strong productivity growth to intensify comparisons of this period to the late -1990s, an episode where Fed Chair Greenspan initially argued for holding back on tightening given his belief that productivity gains would al low for inflation -less growth (though the Fed eventually raised rates from 4.75% to 6.5% during the late -1999/early-2000 period). In a recent report , we detailed the similarities and differences with that episode (see “Why a repeat productivity surge may not be the same panacea for price pressures ”). With respect to the latter, we see other factors, namely a reversal of disinflationary pressures from global and demographic forces, a s limiting the read-through from the Fed’s response in the 1990s to today. records.text: What if 2026 is the year AI Integration goes mainstream in FMCG? Warren Ackerman Barclays, UK Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how staples companies operate, from product development, improving returns on advertising spend and perhaps most crucially how it is being integrated to develop next generation supply chains. AI could be a catalyst to drive efficiency, cut costs, and spark innovation across operations. One area that is already having a big impact is significantly improving supply and demand forecasting accuracy, with a number of FMCG companies reporting big efficiency gains in this area. Best-in-class companies are able to use AI to connect the dots between consumer demand, planning, new product development, supplier relationships, manufacturing and logistics best practice. Creating simplicity in complex FMCG organisation is a key competitive advantage, in our view, as it allows companies to allocate resources better and crucially frees up time from manual tasks to focusing on the real value-add, which is demand generation and driving brand growth. SMEs are also adopting nimble AI solutions with quick returns, providing new operating models that global players can scale up. Market forecasts project outsized growth at a 10yr CAGR of over 37% (Mordor Intelligence, Link) in AI for the consumer staples sector, though estimates vary widely, underscoring both the huge potential and uncertainty in this space. USD HY cyclicals lagged in 2025 even as large‑cap equity cyclicals led, a divergence we attribute to small‑cap cyclicals, which are a closer analogue to HY issuers, staying flat relative to defensives (Exhibit 9). Beyond the outperformance of large banks and tech hardware that propelled large cap cyclical outperformance, our economists expect a front‑loaded cyclical re‑acceleration in 2026 as fiscal tailwinds and easier financial conditions take hold. We see scope for a modest near‑term catchup and broadening out for cyclicals, in line with our Portfolio Strategy colleagues who see upside in equities exposed to middle-income consumers and small caps, at least tactically. Since late November, HY cyclicals have outperformed defensives by just over 50 bp (Exhibit 10). That said, the potential for further labor market weakness remains a notable risk, and sector specific challenges still matter—Packaging and Chemicals continue to face significant headwinds. Net‑net, we think the prospective re‑acceleration is not yet fully priced in HY cyclicals, and that favors a preference toward cyclicals over defensives. records.text: 3. Other Asian economies may need to reassess their growth models. China’s lopsided economic structure—muscular manufacturing, enervated consumption—is a feature of its macro policy and is set to have even bigger global consequences in the years ahead (“China Shock 2.0”). Historically, the fastest-developing economies in Asia shed lower-value manufacturing activities to poorer neighbors as they moved up the technological ladder (this was coined the “flying geese” model, the idea being that less-developed economies like Korea, Taiwan, and eventually ASEAN and China were following behind the most advanced economy—at that time Japan). But dragons don’t fly in formation: China is far larger and its policymakers intend to build as large a manufacturing ecosystem as they can, and to limit the flow of technologies and core manufacturing out of China even as it moves up the value chain. To be sure, some activities like apparel manufacturing and lower-value assembly have moved to Southeast Asia, particularly Vietnam, in part due to US tariff pressures. But China’s policy is to keep as much control of the “means of production” as possible, particularly “core technologies”. Together with a protectionist shift (Exhibit 4) by the single largest export market—the United States—and growing discomfort with the “hollowing out” of manufacturing in Europe, this has major implications for economic models elsewhere in Asia. Common measures of term premium attempt to estimate (b) plus (c) in the context of some model. However, in a sense, the last component (just (c) alone) is also a form of term premi- um; we call it term funding premium (TFP), since it represents the market's price for guaranteeing term funding to the borrower. One place where this term funding premium is directly observable is in the case of Treasury FRNs. These 2-year term floating rate notes (FRNs are currently issued only with a 2-year maturity) pay coupons that are linked to 3M T-bill yields plus a spread. Thus, they produce returns that are similar to a strategy of rolling 3M T-bills over a 2-year horizon, but the (generally positive) spread represents the investor’s compensation for pre-committing to lend for 2 years, as opposed to lending for only 3 months at a time. Our Carry Opportunity Indicator (COI), which includes EM/sovereign/corporate credit, FX, equity volatility and yield curve, is near its lowest levels since the GFC (Exhibit 23). Similar to elevated equity valuations, low carry risk premia alone are not necessarily a warning signal for near-term performance. Carry regimes are closely linked to the business cycle – a high growth score anchors carry risk premia. However, when the growth score is falling to negative levels, indicating a US recession, carry risk trades suffer. For most of 2025, carry risk premia compressed despite a falling growth score due to the unusual Goldilocks backdrop – in 2026, we expect less strong performance for carry trades despite the better growth/inflation mix. Credit usually offers a poor asymmetry late cycle as tight spreads limit upside but there is material downside in case of a recession. Late cycle, more restructuring and releveraging often weighs on credit quality – due to higher rates post the COVID-19 recovery, private sector balance sheets remained healthy (Exhibit 24). This, coupled with high all-in yields, boosted demand for credit. However, recent releveraging in the AI ecosystem increased credit supply and has started to weigh on credit quality. We have studied geopolitical events and risk spikes and found they are often risk-asset buying opportunities – see Geopolitics: Implications for the Economy & Markets for a broad discussion. We tend to look for deeper macro-economic impacts through the prism of potential oil price impact. With the caveat that the leadership situation remains fluid, our commodity strategists see the potential for a large oil price spike as small based on current information. This means we are unlikely to see a risk- asset dip to buy. The classic hedges (gold and VIX) tend to move prior to events and fade quickly thereafter (see quant corner here). In the medium-term, increased supply will likely weigh on oil prices. Given our view of the US administration’s desire to “run-it-hot” and the economy in recovery mode, net-net the headline inflation effects of weaker oil may provide solace to bond markets (and the Fed) supporting equity risk in the coming months. Longer-term, the geopolitical implications are unknown: watch China, Russia and Iran. records.text: Fund flows: Taking stock of credit investor sentiment. 2025 was a solid year for credit funds across the board with USD IG, HY and leveraged loan funds all posting solid inflows for the full year (Exhibit 14). Recently, however, flows into the leveraged parts of the market have softened with outflows equivalent to 0.5% of AUM over Q4 for HY funds and flat for USD loan funds. Keeping with the trend of the last few years, the majority of net flows into USD credit funds went into ETFs rather than mutual funds. In the EUR market, IG funds attracted more inflows than HY funds over the course of 2025 (Exhibit 15). Unlike the USD market, IG funds experienced softness at the end of Q4 rather than HY funds. This week, fund inflows continued with $0.5 billion and $0.8 billion flowing into USD HY and loan funds and $1.2 billion into pure USD IG corporate funds. EUR IG and HY funds also experienced moderate inflows of $0.1 billion and $0.4 billion, respectively. Looking ahead, we expect flows into loan funds will remain subdued as the collective toll of the Fed’s cuts continues to bring down yields on the floating rate asset class and weigh on potential forward carry. records.text: Why was LatAm weak in 2025? 2025 was a tough year for Latin America’s consumer staples, although there were a number of companies that were able to buck the trend, such as Coca Cola and P&G. Brazil, the region’s growth engine, was hit by US tariffs reaching up to 50% on key exports. The resulting uncertainty affected confidence, severely impacting GDP growth, which is expected to come in at c.2%, but well below 2024’s 3.4%. This was compounded by elevated interest rates, which have hovered around 15%, squeezing consumer credit, curbing investment, and prompting retailers to destock. Shoppers in Latin America made fewer trips to stores and have been more willing to switch brands including to private label given squeezed disposable income and persistent food price inflation. Consumers in Brazil have sought value and have been looking for bigger pack sizes and traded down and shopped in more value channels such as cash and carry. In Mexico, remittances from the US after a record $64.7 billion in 2024, reversed an 11-year positive trend, falling by 3-6% as US immigration crackdowns and deportation fears impacted remittance levels. The weakness of the Mexican peso against the US dollar also reduced the value of remittances coming into Mexico. The impact has been quite severe with Mexican household consumption taking a hit, particularly among lower-income groups. Adverse weather piled on further pain. records.text: Asset allocation: Remain modestly pro-risk; expect lower risk-adjusted returns and more breadth We remain modestly pro-risk given a friendly baseline of sturdy global growth, further declines in inflation and continued policy support. That said, we expect reduced tailwinds from monetary policy, with fiscal policy and regulatory easing taking over. In addition, AI tailwinds might shift from capex to adoption, which is likely to keep labour markets weak. Policy uncertainty remains high, e.g. around Russia/Ukraine, US midterm elections, impending Fed changes, US tariffs and China competition. Valuations also remain somewhat elevated and risk premia are compressed, which is typical late cycle. Equities tend to perform well with better growth, policy easing and falling inflation. Having said that, with elevated valuations, risk-adjusted returns are likely to be lower, and we expect performance to broaden out. We prefer equity to credit, which has a worse asymmetry, with upside limited due to tight credit spreads and more downside convexity in case of late-cycle risks. Bonds might become a drag for multi-asset portfolios again, at least in 1H 2026, and are unlikely to provide a large buffer in equity drawdowns. We look for alternative diversifiers and hedges to improve the risk/reward. OW equities with lower but attractive returns expected, potentially with more volatility. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Mixed signals from jewellery demand: Global jewellery demand saw a small rebound in Q3, while India saw a very strong festive season and a surge in imports, suggesting consumers were adjusting to higher prices. However, demand in both China and India softened notably in November. In China, wholesale gold demand was down 32% MoM and 15% YoY, marking the weakest November since 2009 (WGC) with VAT reforms driving gold jewellery costs higher. In India, jewellery volumes weakened too despite strong spending, weighing on imports. We see gold reaching $4,800/oz by year-end, but with risks skewed higher: In our recent price deck, we noted that gold is likely to continue to see macro support - MSe $4,800/oz by 4Q26. We are expecting a slower pace of price increases in 2026 than 2025 (where prices rose over 60%), as higher prices will mean the same amount of money inflow does not buy as much physical gold. Higher prices also bring risks of demand destruction, although we note a strong festive season in India, despite gold rising. If the current momentum and geopolitical uncertainty continue and the USD weakens too, risks are more skewed to the upside than downside. Silver Outlook Silver squeezing, with elevated volatility: Silver rose nearly 150% in 2025, and is already up 7% YTD in the first two days of 2026. records.text: Wage growth is likely to slow further because real incomes are done catching up (Exhibit 11). Our model suggests that labour market tightness is now again the main driver of wage growth. We forecast gains in compensation per employee to slow to 2.9% in 2026Q4, broadly in line with the leading signals from the ECB wage tracker, Indeed posted wages and the ECB SAFE and CTS surveys. Our wage projection is thus consistent with 2% inflation given the underlying 0.5-1% productivity trend. The incoming inflation data have been firmer since the summer, with core inflation at 2.4% in November, mainly reflecting stickier services inflation. That said, core inflation is likely to slow below 2% by the end of 2026 given the effects of the stronger Euro, passthrough from lower energy prices and prospects of a negative inflation effect from Chinese trade rerouting. But at 1.9% in 2026Q4 we expect this undershoot to be modest as the underlying drivers of inflation—including wage growth and inflation expectations—remain consistent with 2% over the medium term (Exhibit 12). records.text: We expect 2026 to be a better year for the Euro area economy than 2025 given n prospects for cyclical improvement. That said, we only look for a small growth improvement as Europe faces several structural headwinds at home and abroad. As a result, we forecast Euro area growth of 1.3% this year with 1.4% on a Q4/Q4 basis (up slightly from last year’s pace of 1.3%) but broadly similar to the consensus. We expect three main factors to drive the cyclical pickup. First, Germany’s fiscal n stimulus is set to provide a significant boost, offsetting contractionary policies elsewhere and resulting in a neutral area-wide fiscal impulse. Second, we expect the negative impact of global trade tensions to diminish, as the drag from tariffs and uncertainty fades. Third, we forecast robust consumer spending, supported by income growth outpacing inflation. Lower energy prices—potentially from a ceasefire in Ukraine—could further bolster consumption. That said, this cyclical improvement is likely to be capped by significant structural n headwinds. In particular, we expect China’s renewed export push to weigh on European trade via rising imports and higher export competition, particularly in Germany and Italy. Increased competition with China reinforces domestic structural headwinds, including high energy costs, underinvestment in high-tech sectors, regulatory burdens, and demographic shifts. records.text: should only be modest in the coming quarters. The resilience of Chinese exports comes from three factors. First, the rapid expansion of Chinese exports to EM economies goes beyond trade rerouting, supported by significant competitiveness of Chinese products and demand generated through China’s outward investment. Second, China’s strong position in rare earths and other critical minerals will likely constrain how far other countries can impose significant trade barriers. Lastly, there is upside potential in high-tech export growth, backed by both policy push and the broad AI-related capex cycle. We expect export price inflation in US dollar terms to turn positive, rising from -2.7% in 2025 to +0.7% in 2026. This reflects both a gradual narrowing of PPI deflation in 2026 and a gradual appreciation of CNY against the USD. In contrast, we expect import growth to be very modest in 2026, with nominal import growth increasing from -0.7% in 2025 to +0.9% in USD terms. We expect goods import volume growth to accelerate from 1.2% in 2025 to 2.5% in 2026, partly reflecting stockpiling of oil for strategic reserves due to the government’s emphasis on national security in key strategic areas. Given declining crude prices, we expect import price inflation to remain negative at -1.6% in 2026 (vs. -1.8% in 2025). records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 05 January 2026 Citi Research 7 The US military operation in Venezuela that removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro should eventually be incrementally bearish for oil market balances, particularly if a more cooperative interim government setup lowers near-term tail risks tied to sanctions enforcement and US policy ambiguity. Indeed, after initial supply losses (covered by our disruption allowance), our base case as published in our annual outlook in Dec’25, assumes Venezuelan production can start rising in 4Q26, by about 0.3 to 0.5-mb/d between mid- 2026 and end-2027. Assuming this timeline, the supply increase could be offset by a gradually tightening global oil supply/demand balance over time, led by OPEC cuts if necessary, alongside demand growth. Some market participants suggest that, with a stable government that can attract investments, oil production could rise by ~0.5-mb/d in about a year, but production increases would be more difficult in subsequent years due to dilapidated infrastructure. The size and pace depend on the magnitude and schedule of any capex increase in the future, contingent on the stability of the country. President Trump’s points on governance and oil made in his interview with Fox News are telling in terms of his drive to see change in Venezuela (The Hill, Jan 3). The governor’s press conference likely signals more confidence in growth recovery from exports, conveying that the BoK sees a balanced, neutral policy rate path ahead. We maintain our no-change view for the rest of this year. Back to fundamentals: We noted earlier that the last window of opportunity for the BoK to cut had passed at the November meeting. As the growth rebound materializes further this year, we see only a thin chance of a cut despite the BoK’s persistent easing bias (see: BoK Review: A Period of Transition). Rather, we think the risk balance for growth is tilted to the upside. Recent strength in tech export demand and the latest BoK issue paper projecting improved private-sector job growth (BoK issue note) – one of the key arguments the dovish dissenter used to call for a cut previously – reinforce this view. Learning from past periods of pre-cycle shift: Looking at historical periods of BoK policy rate pauses, the shift to the opposite monetary policy direction typically occurred after about 15 months on average. Considering the BoK’s last cut in May, this marks eight months of pause despite a clear bias toward a cut over the past six months. We see further room for this flow in 2026 given ongoing regulatory efforts and elevated household cash balances. Arguments: In addition to the planned three-year expansion of equity allocations, Chinese regulators recently introduced a requirement for domestic fund managers to manage their portfolio deviation from benchmark, and for a cut to compensation if underperformance is meaningful. Alongside growth in passive ETF investing, these changes should provide further tailwinds for the popular CSI benchmark indices. We also think policymakers will aim to reduce downside volatility to boost risk- adjusted returns and attract more long-term capital – CSCR Chair Wu Qing picked out the reduction of realised volatility on major indices as a key achievement of the 2021-2025 Five Year Plan. We note sizeable purchases by state-owned funds during market stress in 2025 were not followed up by similar reductions after stabilisation. China onshore interest rates remain quite depressed with one-year big bank deposit rates at 0.95% and 10y CGB yields at 1.85%. Chinese households held CNY163trn of cash deposits as of November 2025, 1.55x the total A-share market capitalisation. The CSI 300 is trading at 14.4x 12m forward P/E, 21% below its 2015 peak. records.text: M Idea 2 Extensive Period of Pause Likely Past period of policy rate pause - on average 15 months We assessed past extended periods of BoK policy rate pauses and expect this time to follow a similar pattern – a pause through the next 18 months. We reviewed the recent pause periods since the GFC, evaluating six instances where the BoK held rates unchanged before shifting to the opposite monetary policy direction or maintaining a meaningful pause longer than a year (e.g., 2013–14). Key patterns during these pause periods across macro variables: • Growth: Real GDP consistently stayed above potential or rebounded from below to above potential in five out of six periods. The exception was 2012, when growth fell below potential but the pause period lasted 12 months before a rate cut appeared. → This time we expect growth to rebound and remain above potential throughout 2026. • Inflation: Headline CPI relative to the target did not show a consistent pattern during pause periods. The BoJ’s estimate for potential growth was around 0.4% in 2022, but has recently risen to 0.66%. If this trend continues, it will theoretically be easier to raise rates. Furthermore, as before, Ueda emphasized the approach of gauging the distance to the neutral rate “from below” each time the policy rate is raised, while carefully assessing the impact on economic activity, prices and financial conditions. He also noted that previous rate hikes have not produced significant tightening effects and that this is one reason to believe that real interest rates remain extremely low. Additionally, he said he does not attach any particular significance to policy rates reaching a 30y high since the inflation environment and other factors differ greatly from past periods. Overall, he did not express the caution seen previously and seemed to indicate a rather proactive stance toward continuing to hike. We expect additional rate hikes in July and December 2026 for the following reasons. records.text: Hong Kong: Domestic demand takes the lead 2025 has been a year of robust growth for the Hong Kong economy. The real GDP growth surprised to the upside over the first three quarters, driven primarily by stronger-than-expected net exports and a pickup in investment growth. The former reflects robust export performance from mainland China despite elevated US tariffs, while the latter likely stems from easing financial conditions – a combination of Fed rate cuts, domestic equity market rally, and the stabilization in the property market. We maintain our 2025 full-year real GDP growth forecast of 3.4%. We expect net exports to contribute +0.5pp to full-year growth in 2025, while investment is projected to contribute 1.8pp. Meanwhile, as non-food goods consumption picked up in 2025 and services consumption grew steadily, private consumption is expected to contribute 0.9pp to full-year growth in 2025 (vs. a 0.5pp drag in 2024; Exhibit 25). Looking ahead, we expect a further recovery in domestic demand – particularly private consumption – to underpin economic growth in 2026 (Exhibit 26). This is supported by a likely continued recovery in property prices, as projected by our Hong Kong real estate team, and a further rally in the equity market expected by our equity strategists. We expect private consumption to contribute 2.2pp to full-year growth in 2026. Continued rate cuts in the US should also lower interest rates in Hong Kong and support investment growth. Heightened global uncertainty impacts de- dollarisation: There is an additional, more structural thematic point for the USD, which ties in with the rising geopolitical risk. Across many countries – with China the most notable example – large current account surpluses are recycled partly through outbound FDI (in US dollars). In a scenario where these investments are perceived to be less safe because of higher geopolitical risk, it could mean less current account recycling (e.g. more converting of USD into local currency). In other words, corporates would sell more US dollars. More generally, in a world where the international community perceives US foreign policy as less predictable, other sovereign nations might be more cautious about transacting in the USD, reducing USD liabilities (borrowing, trade, trade finance) and, over time, assets (FX reserves). Even better risk-reward for steepeners and still bearish duration: The less likely but more market- impactful scenario in which sanctions are lifted and blockades are removed quickly, and oil prices fall significantly and do not recover, would add some nuance to our views. For rates, it would reinforce our expectation of steeper curves in the US, eurozone, and Japan. We hold 1s30s in UST, 10s40s in EUR swaps and 5s10s in JPY swaps. For duration, while we would still maintain an overall bearish slant, such a decline in oil prices might, all else equal, mean yields undershoot our bearish front-end target levels in the US and the eurozone in reaction to more Fed cuts getting priced in and ECB hikes getting priced out. There are two main reasons for this: the delta on Fed policy would be likely to be greater than on the ECB, e.g. we would expect front- end interest rate differentials to move in favour of EURUSD; and the delta on growth would be likely to be more positive for the eurozone than for the US. We estimate that total debt of Venezuela now stands at USD 169 bn, and that 2026 nominal GDP will remain broadly flat at USD 98bn despite increases in oil production due to lower oil prices. This implies a debt/GDP ratio of 173%. We reckon a principal haircut of at least 50% will have to be applied to the external debt. In line with past restructurings and to satisfy the potential IMF conditionality, we assume debt would need to be reduced at least to ~85% debt/GDP at the time of restructuring. Assuming 14% of oil revenue is dedicated to external debt obligations, the new bonds could afford a coupon at around 4.4%. A base case for our analysis is a 20yr ‘new bond’ and a 10yr PDI Bond. After imposing a 50% principal haircut, Venezuela could potentially offer investors a 20yr ‘new bond’ with a 4.4% coupon and a 10yr zero coupon bond for the PDI. Using an exit yield of 11%, the ‘new bond’ NPV would be around 26pts, while PDI bond would be worth on average additional 20pts, bringing the total package to mid-40s. Assessing an implementation of a macro-linked bond linked to the USD nominal GDP of Venezuela yields similar results. The recovery package could increase to the high-40s if an additional contingent instrument (VRIs) like an oil warrant is added. records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Deutsche Bank AG Page 13 The 2026 story - brace for disinflation. Fast-forward a year, we are optimistic about the inflation outlook. Price pressures across the board are easing. Energy prices, we expect will, come down precipitously on the back of Budget measures. Food prices, we expect, will slow. Core goods price momentum, we project, will remain broadly steady at currently subdued rates. And we expect services price momentum to take a big step down in 2026. We go through our detailed projections below. Services: As headline inflation recedes, services price momentum should also gradually fall. Indeed, our suite of underlying services trackers point to easing price pressures. What to expect in 2026? We expect price momentum to pull lower from 4.8% y-o-y this year to 3.2% y-o-y in 2026. By year-end, we expect services inflation to have slowed to sub-3% y-o-y. Indeed, survey data point to slowdown in services price momentum, with the latest PMIs pointing to a meaningful drop in output price expectations. Producer price pressures have also eased from the highs registered in 2023 and 2024. What's driving our projections lower? Household costs for one. Rental inflation we expect will remain subdued - with recent trends in the RICS Residential Survey, HomeLet, Zoopla, and RightMove all pointing to weaker momentum as the official data catches down to the survey data. records.text: Oil Monitor 05 January 2026 Citi Research 2 The US military operation in Venezuela, codenamed “Absolute Resolve” , that removed President Maduro should eventually be incrementally bearish for oil market balances, in our view, particularly if a more cooperative interim government setup lowers near-term tail risks tied to sanctions enforcement and US policy uncertainty. Indeed, after initial supply losses (covered by disruption allowance in our model), our base case as published in our annual outlook in Dec’25, assumes Venezuelan production can start rising in 4Q26, by about 0.3- 0.5-m b/d between mid-2026 and end-2027. Assuming this timeline, the supply increase could be offset by a gradually tightening global oil supply/demand balance over time, led by OPEC+ cuts if necessary, alongside demand growth. Some market participants suggest that, with a stable government that can attract investments, oil production could rise by ~0.5-m b/d in about a year, but more difficult in subsequent years without improved infrastructure. The size and pace of oil supply increase would depend on the magnitude and schedule of capex increases in the future, contingent on political stability in the country. President Trump’s points on governance and oil made in his interview with Fox News are telling in terms of his drive to see change in Venezuela (The Hill, Jan 3). The ongoing property downturn and “anti-involution” policies (which aim to contain disorderly price competition and overcapacity in some industrial sectors) have weighed on property and manufacturing investment, respectively. Fiscal data and anecdotal evidence suggest that government spending has slowed in recent months, with more funds directed towards repaying corporate arrears rather than financing investment projects, resulting in weaker infrastructure investment. However, we would not over-interpret the steepness of the recent slump as our recent study suggests that the NBS statistical correction of previously over-reported data (likely during 2022-24) has played at least as large a role as the above-mentioned fundamental factors. While it’s clear that investment momentum has weakened recently, our analysis suggests the decrease in H2 is less abrupt than what headline FAI data shows, since our investment tracker estimates that China’s real investment growth slowed to around 2.2% yoy in Q4 from 3.7% yoy in H1. Given the ongoing policy easing and a low comparison base, we expect FAI growth to rebound to +2.0% in 2026 from an expected -3.2% in 2025 (Exhibit 15). records.text: s has waned. As Bank Rate has slowly fallen, policy restrictiveness has naturally waned. The pass-through of rate hikes are largely complete, with most corporates and households having already adjusted to higher rates. Indeed, on some of the Bank's models, the policy stance has become "neutral or slightly accommodative". Where do we see R*? Our modelled estimates of the neutral rate have drifted higher this year - but only marginally. Driving some of the increase was a pickup in financial market expectations of where Bank Rate will be - given widening divisions within the MPC through the year. Rising spot CPI hasn't helped either - and neither has stronger growth at the start of the year – all of which have helped push R* higher. Altogether, our estimates of R* come with a wide range: from 2.25% to 3.75% last year, our collection of neutral rate estimates has drifted higher to 2.75% to 3.75%. Looking at the average, our suite of R* estimates have risen slightly from 3.17% to 3.22%. One word of caution: R* estimates are notoriously uncertain and should only be treated as a rough guide, not definitive truth. They're often biased by spot data, notoriously difficult to estimate as latent variables, and highly sensitive to model choices and sampling periods. Furthermore, their accuracy can vary drastically between ex-post and ex-ante calculations, making their use in evaluating policy highly imprecise. records.text: Venezuelan supply remains a source of optionality rather than a structural bearish driver for global oil markets especially near-term. On the China side, if it does not get its typical volumes of Venezuelan oil, then it might have to procure alternative heavy crude oils from the open market – a form of additional buying. Although President Trump did say that Venezuela can continue selling oil, for risk aversion purposes, Chinese buyers could start to buy other heavy oil as substitutes. Over the past year, Venezuelan oil went to the US, China, and Southeast Asia. Much of the world generally does not really see Venezuelan oil, excluding China, and Chevron, which has had US government permission to operate in the country. That’s why oil prices had not moved much before events this past weekend. Some and perhaps much of the Venezuelan oil that goes to Southeast Asia might have ended up in China (Bloomberg, Dec 16). If China doesn’t get Venezuelan oil, then it might have to go to the open market to buy – which means the oil market could get affected. Chinese buyers can certainly take a wait-and-see stance, but hoarding behavior is not out of the question in light of the nature of these events (BBC, Jan 4). Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: The Chinese economy has experienced significant changes in recent years. By n late 2025, China’s export market share in the United States and, domestically, its new property starts, had returned to levels seen in the early 2000s, erasing the gains made since joining the WTO in 2001 and China’s housing reform in 1998. The main challenge for the Chinese economy remains finding new growth engines. Although Chinese exporters have successfully diversified into non-US markets, supporting our positive outlook for Chinese exports, building a consumption- and services-driven economy will take years, if not decades. We expect export volume (real terms) to grow by 5% in 2026, following n approximately 8% real growth in 2025. Strong goods exports, muted imports due to ongoing import substitution, and policies to promote services exports support our forecast that China’s current account surplus will widen from 3.6% of GDP in 2025 to 4.2% in 2026, well above consensus. The property market is likely to continue declining in 2026, but its drag on GDP n should lessen, as the sector’s share of the economy has decreased significantly. Labor market weakness is also expected to persist, driven by both structural factors such as AI- and tech-related job displacement, and cyclical challenges, like the prolonged property downturn. Our 2015 estimate of Venezuela's incentive cost of production (long-run marginal cost) was USD 50/bbl, likely making it economic in today's price environment. What impact on medium term price expectations might this have? Although a sudden supply shock of 1 mmb/d would normally imply an oil price change of roughly 10%, in the base case two factors would lessen the impact: the market's ability to anticipate such an increase well in advance, and the fact that any rise in Venezuela's output would be managed as part of OPEC policy, and potentially limited by quotas. Moreover, under Venezuela’s fiscal regime in 2015 we estimated the royalty per barrel of oil equivalent at USD 13/bbl, which is a relatively high government take, and thus less attractive for international participants. Therefore this would not necessarily change our long term equilibrium price assumption of USD 75/bbl. An alternative scenario where Venezuela exits OPEC, is no longer constrained by quotas, and seeks a production-maximising energy policy whereby international oil majors are incentivized to deploy larger investments, could have a stronger downside impact on medium-term oil prices. 8 "Washington plans to put oil at the heart of Venezuela’s future", Financial Times, 4 Jan 2026, {https:// www.ft.com/content/b395033a-bb3a-4022-a58c-60594e73512c}. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W Better growth in 2026 shouldn’t derail SARB’s disinflationary goals: Our assessment of higher-frequency macroeconomic data in South Africa still points to limited reflationary risks in 2026. Though we expect the economy to grow by a stronger 1.6% in 2026 from an estimated 1.3% in 2025, we think most of the sequential growth impulse is likely to come from stronger fixed investment and a still-supportive net-export outlook on elevated terms of trade rather than an imminent spike in domestic demand. This is likely to lift short-term growth potential in parallel, in our view. Hence, like the SARB, we see a neutral to mildly negative output gap persisting this year. Meanwhile, we think the SARB will be aware of the need to work harder to bring sticky service prices lower. Hence, we don’t expect the SARB to quickly back away from its quarterly projection-model view that 1-year ex-ante real policy rates are only around 50bp away from neutral (Figure 6). South Africa ranks low on reflationary risks compared with EM peers: Outside of our impulse response function and assessment of domestic macro data, our view of relatively low reflationary risks for South Africa is backed up by our quantitative assessment and ranking of reflationary risks among its EM peers – see EM disinflation: Risks to Goldilocks story, dated 17 November 2025. Domestic anchors for prices are likely to still be helped by our expectation for a negative fiscal impulse

Longer-term yields have moved sharply higher, with the 10-year JGB yield now over 2% — above China government yields of similar maturity. Though new Prime Minister Takaichi is a disciple of Abenomics, she is governing in a more constrained era – markets have moved on from their doubts about reflation, and now worry about fiscal sustainability. Catalyst.Metric: Methane emissions reduction via feed additives

records.text: Methane inhibitors on the back foot, and only part of the package Methane inhibitors, a type of food additive, have been touted as a potential silver bullet for methane reduction efforts within dairy. However, they are only projected to reduce emissions by about 5% in the coming years, according to the FAO. Uptake is limited by cost, availability, regulatory barriers, waning effectiveness over time and increasingly public perception and food safety concerns (see, for example, European Chemicals & Ingredients Commoditisation risks revisited). Practical hurdles exist also: additives must be consistently mixed into feed, which is difficult for grazing livestock. Controlled application is essential, as delays between mixing and feeding can reduce effectiveness. And cost remains a significant barrier. Farmers have little direct incentive to adopt additives, which represent an additional expense. Even if these assumptions prove easier to overcome than anticipated, and we are seeing significant innovation happening in this space, broader concerns around feed additives may mean that uptake remains modest. In turn, more complex interventions may be required on farms to compensate. In 2026, attention may start to turn to the consumer companies and their role in funding these alternative initiatives, especially if feed additives take a back seat. More specifically, we think that the store closure program that currently in effect (Kering has already closed 26 Gucci brand stores (net) as of Q3-25) will continue. As a reminder, Gucci has > 500 stores worldwide, similar to the number of Louis Vuitton stores – LV stores 2025 sales are c.EUR25bn. As President Maduro has now been removed, the directional bias points toward higher Venezuelan oil flows availability, but the magnitude and timing of any resulting price pressure remain uncertain and dependent on US policy. The proportion of mortgages with variable interest rates has continued to rise even after the negative interest rate policy was lifted in March 2024 (Figure 3). This suggests that households expect short-term interest rates to remain low. This increases the risk that short-term rates will rise more than households anticipate, which could have unforeseen negative impacts. Additionally, while households' transferable deposits are increasing, their term deposits are decreasing (Figure 4). As there is currently no significant difference between interest rates on ordinary and term deposits, preferring transferable deposits for liquidity reasons is somewhat rational. This rationality is further enhanced if one assumes low interest rates will continue. However, if interest rates rise more than households expect, a rapid shift from transferable deposits to term deposits could occur. records.text: ent and novel way to think about swap spreads across the curve. We summarize our new model in this publication. Our approach begins with the very essence of what swap spreads represent in a world with risk-free benchmark rates. We then add sector-specific elements to fully capture the effects of the drivers of swap spreads in each maturity sector. The term structure of swap spreads embeds term funding premium We begin by noting that swap spreads are essentially a form of term premium. Taking the 10-year sector as an example, it is worth noting that the maturity-matched swap spread (defined as the 10Y swap yield minus the 10Y UST yield) reflects the difference in returns between (i) rolling 1-day risk-free loans in the repo markets for ten years and (ii) a risk-free 10-year term investment in the form of a US Treasury note. Thus, the negative of the swap spread (as we normally define it in the US) can be thought of as a form of term premium. This notion of term premium is different from the term premium that is quantified via met- rics such as ACM term premium. They expect the bull run of Chinese equities will continue, but at a slower pace. Our strategists forecast an annual appreciation of 15-20% for Chinese equities in 2026E and 2027E, underpinned by 14% and 12% profit growth respectively, and ~10% valuation re-rating. Key drivers for potential re-acceleration of profit growth include AI adoption, “Going Global” trends, and “anti-involution” policies. Chinese equities currently trade at meaningful valuation discounts compared to their international peers. The strong diversification value of China for both international and domestic investors should encourage further capital migration into the markets. Short-term rates to trend lower in 2026. We expect the PBOC to deliver two 10bp policy rate cuts in 2026, which would lower the 7-day OMO rate to around 1.2% by end-2026, from 1.4% at end-2025. To facilitate government bond issuance, the central bank is likely to keep interbank liquidity ample, which should bring short-term rates close to the policy rate. By contrast, long-end rates, such as 10y CGB yields, are likely to decline by less than short-term rates, leading to curve steepening. On oil, President Trump said: “We have the greatest oil companies in the world, the biggest, the greatest, and we're going to be very much involved in it.” Yet, is the country stable enough to support a meaningful rise in investments? This hinges on the governance part. On governance, President Trump said: "We can't take a chance in letting somebody else run and just take over where he left off, so we're making that decision now, we'll be involved very much.” This could eventually lead to a scenario of stability in the country. Implementation would be key, but will likely take time and involve considerable risks and unknowns. Near-term expectations of a rapid and large Venezuelan supply surge look anyway overstated, with technical limits dominating the upside. While Venezuela holds vast reserves, the absence of a stable investment climate means large-scale capex-driven growth would take years, not months. Production history underscores this constraint; output peaked at ~ 3.7 mb/d in the ‘70s, hit again a multi-year high of ~ 3.5-mb/d in ‘98, stayed above 2-m b/d in the early ‘10s, then collapsed after the 2014–15 oil price crash. From a trough below 0.3-m b/d in 2020, production has recovered to just over 1-m b/d today, nearly all exported, including via crude-for-products swaps. Sustainability survey suggests climate mitigation remains on the agenda; but methane remains a bit of a blind spot for many In our conversations with European companies exposed to the dairy segment over the course of 2025, including through a sustainability survey shared with European consumer staples companies covered by our fundamental equity team, companies are largely confident to look through the political cycle. They remain conscious of the longer-term trend towards climate change mitigation efforts, and continue to see it as a future policy risk (albeit with a more pragmatic and targeted focus). The fragmented political landscape complicates efforts, however, as managing interventions across diverse regions introduces additional hurdles. But broadly sustainability efforts are still being undertaken at an executive leadership level. In this context, however, we have found that methane emissions is a bit of a blind spot, versus broader initiatives around carbon emissions. Many consumer staples companies are not providing clear targets, nor do they have comprehensive programmes in place to address their methane footprint. There has been some backtracking on specific commitments, too. If methane starts to rise up the agenda in 2026, and pressures start to ramp up, some firms may find themselves on the back foot from a sustainability perspective. 5 January 2026 118 Barclays | Global Consumer Staples

records.text: Fiscal policy: Augmented deficit expansion to continue Following the policy pivot in September 2024 and US tariff increases during February-April 2025, Chinese policymakers have significantly accelerated government bond issuance to secure adequate funding. However, stronger-than-expected exports in 2025 have led to measured government spending. Although our Augmented Fiscal Deficit (AFD) metric widened during Q1-Q3, it narrowed in recent months, and the outstanding fiscal deposit was RMB400bn higher than the year-ago level as of November. This indicates that some government spending planned for 2025 may have been reserved for 2026, given that the 2025 growth target is within reach. December policy meetings indicate continued (albeit measured) fiscal expansion in 2026, and we believe fiscal policy will likely do most of the heavy lifting to stabilize growth. For the 2026 fiscal budget, we expect policymakers to maintain their official on-budget fiscal deficit target at 4.0% of GDP , raise the central government special bond (CGSB) issuance quota to RMB2.0tn from RMB1.8tn in 2025 (including RMB500bn for bank recapitalization in each year), and also increase local government special bond (LGSB) issuance quota to RMB4.8tn from RMB4.4tn in 2025 (Exhibit 19). Fortunately, TFP is still somewhat observable from swap spreads. This is because the 10Y SOFR swap yield (in our example) reflects the sum of (a) and (b). To be sure, swap spreads are not pure measures of term funding premium. In its January 7 research report, the BoK projected private-sector job growth of 120,000 over the next two years versus 50,000 in 2025. This was a key concern for dovish MPC members, who previously cited weakness in the labor market. We also expect the governor to address questions on recent USDKRW moves and December FX measures. records.text: t up, why is 1y1y inflation priced to near perfection versus the Fed’s 2% target? Here’s where the bottom-up story comes in since, from this lens, index construction matters. Pre-COVID, one way to frame core inflation dynamics in the US was that goods were in slight deflation, shelter ran above target and core services ex-shelter adjusted as needed to move overall core near target. Moving forward, this is no longer obviously correct, which is another “core” (pun intended) theme of 2026. Specifically, shelter (which composes more than 40% of core CPI) cannot necessarily be relied upon to make up for weak goods inflation. CPI rents and OER inflation have already slowed to, or below, the pre-COVID trend, and private metrics imply the potential for additional slowing to come. The Zillow rent index, which grew around 4% y/y from 2012 through 2019, ran closer to 3% from mid-2023 to mid-2025, and has decelerated further in recent months. Measuring the precise timing and passthrough into CPI rents is difficult, but the direction of travel is intuitive. To take the logic one step further, if shelter inflation runs below the pre-COVID trend, this means that “supercore” inflation (a key sub component closely monitored by FOMC officials composed of services which are especially labor market sensitive) likely must sustainably run higher in order to offset. Between 5-10 cents of every US AI investment dollar ends up in Taiwan: about half of US AI investment is in compute, with Nvidia capturing a huge fraction of this; much of the rest finds its way to Asia, with TSMC the single biggest supplier. Consensus growth forecasts for 2025 GDP growth in Taiwan were 2.9% at the beginning of the year and are now 6.7% (we forecast 7.8%, and a well-above-consensus 4.4% in 2026); effectively all of this is due to blowout export growth (+56% yoy as of November), which in turn is dominated by tech products. Korea sees about 1/4 as much revenue from overall semiconductor sales as Taiwan, with growth driven by demand for high-bandwidth memory chips; with an economy that is twice as big, its GDP boost from AI/tech investment is much more modest. Beyond the outperformance of Taiwan and Korea’s leading tech firms, competition from Chinese manufacturers is intense, limiting margins and growth. Domestically, both these economies face typical East Asian challenges. The working-age population has been declining for the better part of a decade, and household debt levels are quite high, particularly in Korea. Domestic demand growth has been sluggish, aside from investment in tech production and short-term stimulus. On oil, President Trump said: “We have the greatest oil companies in the world, the biggest, the greatest, and we're going to be very much involved in it.” Yet, is the country stable enough to support a meaningful rise in investments? This hinges on the governance part. On governance, President Trump said: "We can't take a chance in letting somebody else run and just take over where he left off, so we're making that decision now, we'll be involved very much.” This could eventually lead to a scenario of stability in the country. Implementation would be key, but will likely take time and involve considerable risks and unknowns. Near-term expectations of a rapid and large Venezuelan supply surge look anyway overstated to us, with technical limits dominating the upside. While Venezuela holds vast reserves, the absence of a stable investment climate means large-scale capex-driven growth would likely take years, not months. Production history underscores this constraint: Output peaked at ~ 3.7-m b/d in the ‘70s, hit again a multi-year high of ~ 3.5-m b/d in ‘98, stayed above 2-m b/d in the early ‘10s, then collapsed after the 2014–15 oil price crash. From a trough below 0.3-m b/d in 2020, production has recovered to just over 1-m b/d today, nearly all exported, including via crude-for-products swaps. The market should now start expecting the slope of the SGD NEER band to steepen 50bp by the MAS’s April 2026 meeting, in our view. An adjustment could be made even in the January meeting, if the MAS wants to stay ahead of the curve. We think the MAS’s rationale could be straightforward: stronger growth and rising core inflation warrant less loose monetary settings, and a steeper SGD NEER slope provides a clean mechanism to achieve that. SGD NEER: An increase in the SGD NEER slope will have immediate implications for investors, in our view. Rather than declaring Nicolás Maduro formally removed—an outcome that would have forced near-term elections—the judiciary opted for a bespoke legal construct that preserves institutional order. This approach underscores a likely preference for administrative stability and strongly suggests that Rodríguez’s initial mandate will be prolonged, with elections deferred as part of a potentially gradual, negotiated transition. However, President Trump has indicated she “is willing to do whatever is needed, ” after a conversation with Secretary Rubio (AP , 1/3/26). It will be important to monitor how Maduro's capture impacts the military leadership. Any moves towards a real political transition (potentially culminating in general elections still in 2026) will be highly scrutinized by investors. Morgan Strategic Research We see a continued unequal K-shaped economy, propelled by asset reflation, with AI amplifying polarization even further. Higher-income households continue to drive a disproportionate share of spending, supported by wealth gains and stable employment. Lower-income consumers remain strained by sticky inflation, and weak job growth is most pronounced among young workers. Figure 13T o p 3 0 % o f i n c o m e e a r n e r s a c c o u n t f o r o v e r 5 0 % o f t o t a l c o n s u m p t i o n shows that the top 30% of income earners account for over 50% of consumption. Our global economics team notes the decline in the savings rate as wealth gains translate into consumer spending through the “wealth effect.” As household wealth rises, households are less constrained to save out of their income, allowing them to increase spending even absent an increase in income. This effect has historically averaged around 3.5 in the US. That is, for every $1 gain in wealth, US households spend an additional $0.035 of their income. records.text: Multi-asset volatility: Late cycle hedging for up and downside In late-cycle backdrops, investors need to be selective about risk management strategies. Investors need to optimise the cost/risk reduction trade-off – how much strategies cost and how well they work when needed. While we do not think AI stocks are in a bubble...yet, the 1996-2002 period can still provide a useful case study for hedging bubble risk. Exhibit 43 shows the excess return (vs. cash) of the S&P 500 with different risk management overlays (leveraged to match the volatility of the S&P 500 over 1996-2002 for a better comparison). The excess return over the 1996-1999 period highlights the carry of each overlay during the rally, while the excess return over the 1996-2002 period highlights the protection (after cumulative carry) they provided. Overall, systematic momentum overlays, longer-dated call options, CTAs, defensive/quality stocks, and bonds performed the best, while traditional ‘safe havens’ underperformed. In 2025, few systematic option overlays helped performance (Exhibit 44). Outside of the sharp equity drawdown around Liberation day, volatility has generally been relatively anchored. In that environment, most equity option overlays struggled to justify their negative carry, underperforming an unhedged S&P 500 position on both an absolute and risk-adjusted basis. records.text: The property sector is now in its fifth year of decline, with most property activity indicators – such as new home starts, sales, and property investment – down 50-80% from their 2020-21 peaks (Exhibit 8). Home prices have also fallen faster in recent quarters, in both primary and secondary markets. We expect continued housing easing in 2026, including further reductions to mortgage rates, further relaxation on home purchase restrictions in Tier-1 cities, and increased policy support for urban village renovation and local government purchases of housing inventories. However, we see no sign of a near-term property sector bottoming out, as housing inventory remains elevated (especially in lower-tier cities), the pass-through from slumping home starts to property construction and investment continues, some large developers (e.g., Vanke) still face challenging funding conditions, and there appears to be no “quick fix” for the property sector. The growing financial losses of the unprecedented property downturn will have to be shared among households, developers, financial institutions and local governments. Should China follow the typical housing bust timeline implied by global experiences, there might be another 10% home price correction ahead and real prices may not bottom out nationwide until 2027, according to our previous study. By using high-speed cameras and trained AI models, Mondelēz can detect anomalies or sub-standard products in real time and optimise gas consumption. About 6% of USD HY and 6% of EUR HY bonds are in distress under our definition of sub‑5‑year maturities and either spreads above 1,000 bp or prices below 80 cents on the dollar. That sits near the 30th percentile of the post‑GFC distribution, elevated relative to index‑level HY spreads near post‑COVID lows (Exhibit 11). By contrast, in USD HY the persistence of distress is closer to history—about 60%—but the tail is more sector skewed, with TMT dominating (right panel, Exhibit 13). A slow‑moving, idiosyncratic EUR HY cohort and a TMT‑heavy USD HY tail which embeds secular risks, both offer limited beta to better macro conditions. We remain underweight CCCs in both markets. records.text: US Economics 05 January 2026 Citi Research 3 individuals forgo insurance altogether, but we do not expect much immediate or substantial impact on health services prices. Health insurance premiums are a much larger share of CPI inflation (around 0.8% of headline, 1% of core). In theory, as CPI measures out-of-pocket expenditures, there would be a boost to CPI from higher premiums. But in practice, we are not expecting an impact on health insurance CPI from higher ACA premiums. Health insurance in CPI is calculated as the “retained earnings” of insurance companies, i.e., a function of health insurance premiums less the cost of benefits paid out. ACA subsidies lowered the cost for consumers through a subsidy given to insurance companies. There should not be a change in overall premiums received by insurance companies, whether the total amount is paid by consumers or by the government. If there is some modest effect on health insurance in CPI, we would not expect this to be noticeable until the second half of the year at the earliest. Industry data used to calculate health insurance is incorporated into CPI with a lag. Data for the first half of 2026 would not be available until the summer and likely not incorporated into CPI until at least Q4 2026. Figure 1. Inflation forecasts and details © 2026 Citigroup Inc. Source: Citi Research Estimates In line with recent restructurings, the idea of MLBs would fit Venezuela’s growth outlook. A restructuring could enhance creditor recovery while preserving near- term liquidity by pairing a new base bond with a Value Recovery Instrument (VRI) or offering a Macro-linked Bond. The IMF has increasingly supported state- contingent features in high-volatility cases: Sri Lanka’s proposed Macro-Linked Bonds adjust coupons to nominal GDP performance (See: Sri Lanka Economics & Strategy: The Final Stretch of Debt Restructuring); Zambia introduced commodity- linked triggers tied to copper revenues; and Suriname adopted macro step-ups linked to external solvency improvements. Common across these cases is that upside is back-loaded and only realized if the sovereign’s capacity to pay improves. For Venezuela, a similar approach could link payouts to net oil export receipts or government oil take, verified by independent reporting. This structure preserves stabilization space early in the program while offering conditional upside to investors.
