records.text: Dwyfor Evans 6 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General EM Inf lation in Focu s : Play it again Credibility remains intact as disinflation meets caution . This remains a supportive inflation backdrop for EM. Inflation trends continue to moderate, fuel prices are softer, albeit less so with food, but the rates buffer that EM central banks have built offers some scope to continue the rate easing path. Several EM central banks eased rates in December – the second highest monthly total of net easing in the year – and yet sufficient caution continued to underpin policy credibility. The upshot is that the strong performance of EM sovereign rates in 2025 has been built on solid foundation and many EM – Brazil and South Africa are the standouts for us – continued to offer value as we head into another year. LatAm. Monthly online prices from the Brazil PriceStats series moderated into year-end and the annual inflation rate slowed further to 4.1%. This is lowest yoy reading for Brazil online prices since November 2024. A policy rate of 15% thus implies an extremely elevated real interest rate >10%. The rates market had priced in a modest rate ease for the 29 January COPOM meeting, but the BCBs hawkish stance in mid -December drove a flattening in the DI curve and reinfor ces a perception of prolonged tight policy. records.text: In 1H 2026, more positive growth momentum might trigger a more procyclical shift across assets. Historically positive growth momentum tends to boost equity vs. bond performance and drives procyclical rotations across and within assets (Exhibit 12). Due to policy support, equities already performed strongly in 2025 even though US growth momentum was negative due to tariffs and the government shutdown. In 2026, equity returns may be lower, especially in risk-adjusted terms, despite a more friendly macro backdrop. While not our baseline, with some late-cycle features, there is potential for concerns on inflation and policy tightening, especially in 1H 2026 when US growth is particularly strong. Also, equity and credit risk premia are lower, as is common late cycle – even with strong growth momentum, absolute equity returns might be constrained by valuations (Exhibit 13). The impact extends beyond direct replacement, as many companies are reassessing future labor needs in light of AI capabilities, creating additional uncertainty for job seekers, particularly young workers and new graduates. While overall unemployment rates have not moved significantly yet, the risk of displacement and wage pressure is rising as AI adoption accelerates (see 2026 Outlook: Consumer & Specialty Finance, Richard Shane, 4 Dec 2025). Recent survey data show that 32% of US workers use generative AI weekly for work, with 13% using it daily. Users estimate that without AI, they would need to work about 5% more hours, translating to a 1.2% gain in productivity. Time savings are positively correlated with income, suggesting that AI enhances "effective labor supply" more for higher-income workers. However, the aggregate impact could be larger if firms are adopting AI in ways not captured by household surveys, such as automating customer service before human intervention is needed (see US Weekly Prospects, Michael Feroli, 28 Nov 2025). Our basecase for 2026: greenshoots of a labour market recovery to emerge in spring bringing some stabilisation. We expect a gradual recovery in the labour market over 2026, with some greenshoots emerging around spring. But we expect hiring plans to remain choppy for much of the year. Instead, the US unemployment rate was up 0.5pp in 2025 through November. That gap alone represents more than one and a half million jobs. The 2025 experience shows that with robust productivity growth, solid growth can be sustained even with a loosening labor market. At some level, this is consistent with a positive technological/supply shock (more output, less price pressure) resulting from AI. And, if this is indeed the case, we could see more of the same in 2026, which seems to be what markets are pricing. But the risk is that markets have a recency bias and are naively assuming the same dynamics persist this year. Indeed, a major risk in the coming quarters is that Okun’s law begins to reassert itself – labor markets tighten and wage growth accelerates. records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Page 18 Deutsche Bank AG The dovish scenario. What's the dovish scenario? A further - and perhaps non-linear - easing of the labour market given the stalled jobs recovery could lead to a further and possibly quicker injection of monetary policy stimulus. Indeed, the latest PMI data point to a very weak jobs recovery. The latest DMP survey also points to muted hiring intentions - broadly similar to what the KPMG/REC survey shows. Combined with some acceleration in AI/digitalisation, it's conceivable to see continued protracted weakness in the labour market. Furthermore, the drop in CPI could also lead to falling inflation expectations, with private sector pay settlements for next year tracking closer to 3% as opposed to the Bank Agent's preliminary 3.5% reading. The hawkish scenario. What's the hawkish scenario? Simply, any rate cuts in 2026 will require a larger accumulation of evidence to unwind any remaining policy restrictiveness. Politics: Timing of dissolution and general election is key The main political focus is, above all, the timing of the lower house dissolution and general election. The Takaichi administration’s approval rating is extremely high at around 75%, but such ratings are usually highest immediately after a new administration is launched and then clearly tend to decline over time (Figure 22). This time as well, the dissolution is widely expected to come while approval ratings remain high. In addition, PM Takaichi’s term as president of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) runs until September 2027, but there will be unified local elections in the spring of 2027. Short-term upside seems overwhelmingly on the blending/diluent side rather than political, with diluent availability the key swing factor for incremental barrels. Near-term gains likely hinge on access to naphtha to blend with and dilute extra-heavy crude as “diluent” . A return of US naphtha and other diluents should ease bottlenecks created by expensive and unreliable alternatives, unlocking up to ~200-k b/d of incremental output without meaningful new investments. These barrels would clear at a discount, but they are real and fast. This likely remains the only credible short-cycle upside, largely independent of broader political change, though still reliant on sanctions relief and logistical normalization. Incremental heavy oil barrels would be well received by US Gulf Coast refineries, displacing alternatives such as Canadian oil imports, perhaps toward China. records.text: (4) Late-cycle valuation frustration While the broad macro backdrop is getting more supportive, valuations across risky assets are elevated, which is typical late cycle. The S&P 500 Shiller P/E is at levels last seen at the end of 2021, during the Tech Bubble in the late 1990s, the Nifty 50 Bubble in the 1960s and the Golden 20s (Exhibit 14). Similarly, positioning and sentiment are again more bullish into 2026 (see also Multi-asset positioning section). And this is despite relatively high US 10-year bond yields, suggesting some of the lowest equity risk premia outside the Tech Bubble. Most non-US equity markets are also trading above their long-run average. As we wrote in our strategic tilting framework, long-term equity returns are likely to be lower than average in most macro scenarios outside those with very bullish AI impacts. However, valuations on their own are not necessarily a good signal for market timing for the near term. Equity valuations can stay high as long as macro conditions remain favourable. S&P 500 Shiller P/Es often increased and were higher when being more late cycle (Exhibit 15). During late-cycle slowdowns with policy easing and anchored inflation, such as those of the late 1990s and mid-60s, equity valuations were supported by structural optimism around new technologies, similar to AI right now. records.text: We expect the year-over-year growth of household real consumption to moderate to 4.5% in 2026 from 4.8% in 2025. A weak labor market has constrained households’ ability to spend. Continued declines in house prices have negatively impacted consumer confidence. As a result, household “excess deposit”, defined as the extra household bank deposits above pre-Covid trend, continued to increase. That said, these deposits imply room for further funds reallocation, should macro and market conditions turn more favorable. China’s equity market rallied by around 20% in Q3 and there appeared to be some green shoots in the high-end retail market in recent months. PBOC data indicates that more households are interested in investing in the stock market, suggesting slightly improved risk appetite. On the back of the RMB 10tn local government debt resolution plan launched in late 2024, growth in government consumption – which accounts for 30% of total consumption – accelerated from 0.8% in 2024 to 4.0% in 2025 by our estimates. Looking ahead, we expect government consumption growth to further increase to 5.0% in 2026, supported by further fiscal expansion as well as an increased policy emphasis on “investing in people” (投资于人, meaning education and healthcare) vs. “investing in things” (投资于物, meaning traditional infrastructure). Overall, the contribution of total consumption, comprising both household and government segments, to headline GDP growth is projected to remain flat at 2.6pp in 2026.

We think this boils down to either a) running a largeer balance sheet to limit repo pressures a priori, or b) responding to repo pressures ex-post by added reserves in something of a make-up strategy. But we see pitfalls with either of these tactics. Taken to its logical conclusion, the former means the Fed would run reserves at a level to accommodate the most extreme expected swings in the TGA (such as around the April tax filing deadline) and still have ample reserves without relying on SRP to make up any shortfall. That implies that for much of the rest of the time, and after the TGA declines, reserves are likely to be higher than necessary. A version of this RMP structure was how we interpreted the communications from the December FOMC, with the Fed ramping up T-bill purchases now, in anticipation of a sharp rise in the TGA come April, and then a lowering to a longer-run steady state level of purchases thereafter. Moreover, given the stigma issues over the SRP that emerged in Q4, the Fed seemed more hesitant to rely on it to maintain rate control. The second of these two views suggests a framework in which the Fed runs reserves at a lower level and relies on greater use of its standing repo operations to handle fluctuations in the TGA. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 05 January 2026 Citi Research 6 On the economic front, a more stable Venezuela would be positive for Colombia in the medium and long run. Before relations between the neighboring nations soured, Venezuela represented 15% of all Colombian exports. This has since fallen virtually to zero (in official figures). Regime change and return to credible democratic processes could bring back an important source of demand for agricultural goods and services. Migration flows could move in either direction depending on how fast the situation evolves, but Colombia has already received and formalized the migration situation of around 3mn Venezuelan migrants during Maduro’s regime. This suggests the shock has already been strong, and the Colombian government has been able to weather it. On the oil front, while our take overall points toward somewhat lower oil prices, Colombian oil production has fallen under President Petro, diesel remains subsidized, and a shortage of gas (broadly used for heating and cooking) is looming. Hence, a fall in energy costs is not necessarily a strong negative overall. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Silver and Gold ended near the top of the leaderboard – copper also rallied after relatively poor performance in 2024. The same has been true with Bitcoin, which ended last year down 10% after the 123% rally in 2024. records.text: What if Sir Dave Lewis transforms Diageo? Laurence Whyatt Barclays, UK Sir Dave Lewis starts as CEO on 1 January 2026, joining an industry which is facing its fair share of challenges. Diageo’s share price is at levels not seen in the past decade, and expectations of volume growth in the US alcohol industry are barely seen. It is fair to say that he will have a lot on his plate. Similarities between Tesco then, and Diageo now On the surface, there are few similarities between Tesco’s retail business and Diageo. However, from speaking to our colleagues in Food Retail, who knew Lewis from his time at Tesco, the first major problem that presented itself to Lewis at that time was the rise of hard-discount supermarkets in the UK. Consumers had been financially squeezed and were looking for value alternatives. Today’s alcohol market in the US has echoes of this: the rise of Ready-to-Drink brands is partially driven by the low unit price when compared to a full-size bottle of spirit. Of course, the volume is different, as well as the number of serves per unit, but the unit price is lower. For a consumer living pay cheque to pay cheque, that is what matters. So we see an opportunity for Lewis to use his experience in competing for financially challenged consumers as particularly important at Diageo. Since the benchmark transition, swap spreads have become more tricky to model in a stable fashion. To a considerable extent, this is because SOFR does not contain a credit element like Libor did, and that has made SOFR swap spreads somewhat less “macro” in nature. Instead, swap spreads - which now represent the differential between a risk-free Treasury bond yield and expectations for a risk-free benchmark rate - have become much more nuanced. Additionally, there appear to be macro phenomena that impact all swap spreads in a way that is not fully captured by focusing on swap spreads in individual maturity sectors. This suggests that a more holistic approach is needed to understand the behavior of swap spreads across the curve. To address this limitation, we have developed a fundamentally different and novel way to think about swap spreads across the curve. We summarize our new model in this publication. Morgan Modeling term funding premium Thus far, this measure of term funding premium is merely a distilled version of the term structure of swap spreads. We must find a way to model TFP based on the underlying fundamental drivers for it to be a useful framework for modeling swap spreads themselves. We do this below. One might logically expect this term funding premium to depend on factors that reflect sup- ply and demand. This is indeed the case, and we include five factors that help explain the variation in TFP over the past five years. The underlying drivers that we use are the follow- ing: • Cost of leverage, which we define as the total marketable debt (minus the Fed’s SOMA portfolio) versus the size of the Fed’s balance sheet. This factor is intended to capture supply within the context of the liquidity that is available in the system to absorb it • WAM of Treasury securities, to capture Treasury debt management strategy decisions, as increases (or decreases) in coupon auction sizes would result in an expectation for this WAM to increase (or decrease) • Commercial bank deposits, to capture bank demand for USTs, as there is a strong rela- tionship between deposit growth and bank holdings of UST

The latest projection forecasts Q1 2026 inflation at 1.9% y/y and a new low of 1.8 % y/y in Q4 2026. Consequently, we estimate that headline inflation would have to shift at least 40bp to match the low at which the ECB opted not to cut. Based on our current passthrough estimates, achieving such a reduction would require oil prices to fall by 23% (to USD47/bbl), while a 50bp reduction would demand a 29% drop (to USD43/bbl). At face value, then, our assumption of a short-lived fall in oil prices to USD50/bbl would not cross this threshold. Our bias would therefore be that the ECB keeps rates on hold (our base case sees the next move being a hike in Q3 2027). However, we think policymakers would be particularly attentive to signs that low energy prices were filtering into wider wage and price-setting behaviour. With profit margins currently compressing, we believe such disinflationary second-round effects would be muted. If such signs were to emerge, though, impetus for another rate cut could grow. Per its disclosures, Altria had $24mn (Q2) and $20mn (Q3) excise tax benefit from double duty drawback, which is c3% of its US cig vols (vs 0% last year). This duty drawback could potentially be a significant source of income for Altria, in our view. We know that it aims to sell c3bn of cig packs in FY25 and would pay c$3bn in federal excise taxes. Theoretically, if Altria were able to use this duty drawback on 100% of its cig vols (without raising a lot of conflict with IRS and stakeholders at large), we estimate it could potentially see a $3bn EBIT benefit. We are not necessarily drawing a 1:1 connection between Basic and the duty drawback, but, from an economics perspective, we think it would be a good opportunity if Altria could reinvest some of its gains in its cig business (e.g. within its deep discount business). What does this mean in the context of volume share? Altria is likely to see the biggest relative benefit, in our view. Q3 25 demonstrated the success MO is having in deep discount, and the company has the opportunity to make use of its duty drawback benefit to offset any losses from this push on Basic. Deep discount aside, YTD MO has had a volume share of c45% vs. BATS at c29%, IMB at c10% and JT at c7% in US cigs. records.text: (5) Lowdown on the risk of an equity drawdown For the medium term, equity asymmetry appears negatively skewed, which is typical in late-cycle backdrops. Based on our equity asymmetry framework, the risk of a large equity rally in the next 12 months is low as those usually occur from low valuations and during early cycle recoveries (Exhibit 17). Normally, late in the cycle, with economies operating near full capacity and elevated valuations, upside for risk assets is increasingly limited. records.text: Monetary policy: A measured and flexible approach to easing In response to US tariffs on Chinese products, the PBOC announced a package of easing measures in early May aimed at stabilizing market expectations, including a 10bp policy rate cut and a 50bp RRR cut. However, since then the central bank has repeatedly emphasized a cautious approach toward further monetary easing. Policy communication from the PBOC has reinforced a data-dependent framework, pointing to a reactive rather than proactive easing approach. Consistent with this, recent statements have shifted emphasis from near-term growth headwinds to medium-term economic dynamics, underscoring policymakers’ preference for preserving policy room. The cautious stance reflects the PBOC’s balancing act between providing growth support and safeguarding financial stability. Banks’ net interest margins continue to compress, limiting the scope for policy rate cuts, especially given rising concerns over the health of the banking system. Meanwhile, the PBOC retains a broad set of alternative tools to manage liquidity conditions, including OMOs, MLF loans, outright reverse repos, and CGB purchases. Fiscal subsidies to interest payments could also partially substitute for policy rate cuts. records.text: comes as a by-product of other metal extraction, namely lead/zinc (29%), copper (27%) and gold (15.5%) mining. This means mine supply is less likely to react to silver price signals alone. Global mined output has in fact shown a flat to declining trend over the last decade (- 0.7% CAGR), led by declines in Australia, Peru, and North America. Of the contributions to mine supply, only that from copper has seen growth over the last 10 years (+1.5% CAGR 2015-2024). Over the same period, silver from lead/zinc mining has fallen by 0.8% CAGR on mine closures, and that from gold by 1.7%. At the same time, mine output has become even more weighted to by-product supply, with the share of primary silver mines falling by 4.7 percentage points since 2015 to 27.75% in 2024. Mexico is the largest producer, with Jan-Oct 2025 output up 3.7% YoY, but production has been challenged by changing mining laws and permitting difficulties in recent years. However, some reports suggest this has been improving in 2025, potentially leaving room for some more growth ahead. Zinc is also seeing mine supply growth for the first time in a few years, although supply disruptions in copper are mounting up, leaving a mixed picture for the silver supply outlook.

records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Page 12 Deutsche Bank AG The Inflation Outlook - Swift Disinflation n We expect inflation to take a big step down in 2026. Budget measures around the cost of living help lower household bills. And with wage pressures easing, we expect much of the one-off level increase in payroll taxes to wash out of the inflation data in 2026. Still, some stubborn increases in price momentum will likely remain given indexation effects. We expect headline CPI to average 2.4% y-o-y next year, and RPI to average 3.3% y-o-y. The 2025 inflation story was marred by many one-offs. In a nutshell, 2025 inflation was largely as expected. Coming into the year, we expected CPI to run near 3.5% y-o-y. With 11 months of data to hand, we now think headline CPI will average 3.4% y-o-y. The Chancellor's maiden Budget added roughly 0.6pp to 1pp to headline CPI, with big increases in payroll tax, VAT bills, regulatory costs, duties, and index-linked price changes lifting inflation meaningfully. records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Page 8 Deutsche Bank AG The Labour Market Outlook - A Very Uncertain Jobs Recovery n Despite the increase in slack, we expect greenshoots in the labour market to emerge by spring. But a labour market recovery is not assured. The path ahead remains bumpy. Hiring plans remain stalled. Expectations remain weak. And supply side concerns are likely to pick up as mismatches rise again. Increased automation, digitalisation and the advent of AI, we think, are likely to push NAURU higher. On wages, we expect wage growth to remain on a downtrend pulling to 3% by the end of 2026. The 2025 story saw a double whammy of redundancies and increased participation. Unemployment saw a surge in 2025, rising 0.7pp to a new cyclical high of 5.1% (as of October 2025). The UK redundancy (gross) level also picked up to over 100k per month. HMRC data highlighted a fall in pay-rolled employees of over 150k. And the Workforce Jobs data was consistent with a more modest 57k fall in employees. While much of the focus has been on redundancies, 2025 was also very much a story of a higher participation. In fact, outside the early 1980s, labour force participation registered its fastest growth on record. And the share of marginally attached workers (i.e. workers outside the labour market who want a job) has also hit a cyclical high. But this was in part due to idiosyncratic spikes in temporary layoffs and labor force reentrants. The LFPR also rose a tenth to 62.5% (we expect it to decline to 62.4% Dec). Hence, we expect the u-rate to decline a tenth to 4.5% with risks of rounding to 4.4%. Fed: all eyes on the u-rate The Fed’s Jan decision will likely hinge on the Dec u-rate. A print of 4.5% or lower should keep the Fed comfortably on hold, while 4.7% or higher would point to further labor deterioration and probably precipitate a cut. 4.6% is a close call. Scenarios for oil: While there remains major uncertainty on the near future of the current regime as well as US involvement in the country’s administration, we delineate two scenarios: 1) a smooth transition to a new leadership still supported by members of the old regime, or to a US administration until elections; and 2) civil unrest under either a US or new administration, or an increase in tensions with the US, hindering the recovery of the oil production. Scenario 1 is the most likely, in our view, and our central case. It assumes that changes in sanctions and blockages relief in Venezuela on Q2 2026, with only a gradual production recovery (see Global Macro: Impact of Venezuelan regime shift, 8 January). This scenario does not alter the core market views we outlined in Global Outlook 2026 on 28 November, but it adds a downside to oil prices throughout the year as sanctions are lifted in the future and supply from Venezuela slowly recovers. In the less likely but more market-impactful scenario in which sanctions are lifted sooner and production ramps up faster, oil prices could fall significantly and quickly, with impacts on FX and monetary policy. Scenario 2 would entail not only no lifting of the sanctions, but possibly some hit on oil production that could lead to limited upside impact on oil prices. records.text: 9. Private investment is key to drive India’s expansion in 2026 and beyond. A self-imposed slowdown in 2023-24 — via a combination of tighter monetary, credit, and fiscal policies — has largely come to an end. Goods exports face a challenge from very high US tariffs. Government infrastructure spending has been significant in recent years but is now fading. With tighter credit regulation having played out, interest rates lower, and liquidity conditions benign, the decline in household credit growth seems to have bottomed out. With the currency somewhat more competitive, and healthier bank and corporate balance sheets, conditions are fertile for a rebound in private investment. A wider current account deficit and slower portfolio inflows weighed on the currency, along with a somewhat more flexible FX management approach from the RBI. We think the bulk of INR underperformance is behind us, however: we continue to expect a resolution that brings the average US tariff rate down to 15-20% and helps capital flows recover; we also anticipate that the RBI will be less comfortable with significant FX depreciation from here. 10. AWE Private Regular Pay growth we think will slow to 3.5% in Q4-25 before dropping further to around 3.25% in Q4-26. We will be watching for two things in the new year. On the former, we expect private pay pressures to be tempered - albeit marginally. On the latter, we expect public sector pay deals to also narrow with the private sector growth over the coming year. This is because the swap rate reflects the annualized return that can be locked in today via a strategy of rolling overnight risk-free loans over some horizon (say, 10 years), while the corresponding Treasury yield reflects the return on a term risk-free loan over that same horizon. The swap spread, being the difference between the two, is a reflection of the premium associ- ated with committing funding to term • This “term funding premium” (or TFP for short) is directly visible in the case of Treasury FRNs, which are floating rate notes that are linked to 3M T-bills but typically price and trade at a positive spread over that benchmark. This positive spread is the investor’s compensation for lending for a 2Y period rather than rolling 3M T-bills - term funding premium, in other words. records.text: nities. Base Metals Copper Outlook US imports are keeping ex-US markets tight: US copper imports are surging again, reaching a weekly record of 67 kt for the week ending 18 December. COMEX copper inventories have reached an all-time high of 490k short tons, but remain well below total warehouse capacity of ~1.12 mln short tons, implying no constraint near-term to this flow continuing. This is keeping ex-US markets tight, with the LME curve in backwardation and warehouse inventories low. Copper price strength depends on the US tariff path: The US Secretary of Commerce has recommended a phased universal tariff on refined copper of 15% starting in 2027, rising to 30% in 2028. The Secretary is due to provide an update to President Trump by June 30, 2026, so that the President may determine whether a phased import duty on refined copper is warranted. As such, the pull of metal to the US is likely to continue through at least June 2026 and we think it is very unlikely that any metal will be exported, making the US stockpile more like a strategic reserve for now. The biggest downside risk to copper would be if the US were to rule out refined copper tariffs entirely, releasing these volumes. In the US, 3Q25 data proved the continued strength of the US economy before the final rollout of tariffs, with private final domestic demand printing a healthy 3.0% q/ q saar (with a solid 3.5% for personal consumption expenditures). Hidden in the depths of the Q3 GDP print, however, was evidence that firms are now starting to push tariff costs to consumers rather than taking the cost on the margin. And so even as the initial read on the nominal spending data for October showed strength, we are still tracking a slowdown in real consumption growth in 4Q25 relative to the previous quarter. While any slowdown is forecast to be modest since the Fed has already started cutting and fiscal stimulus lays ahead, the contours of the data, nevertheless, will affect the Fed. Indeed, our Fed call is closely tied to the sequencing of growth in the coming months. We hold our January cut but recognize that data needs to cooperate. The broader point is that the Fed is likely to be highly reactive to the data in the next few meetings – notwithstanding the change at the helm of the Fed in the coming months. records.text: What if PFAS bans take effect? Amy Lian Barclays, UK | Hannah Greenberg BCI, US PFAS, also known as "forever chemicals" (and short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), are a group of chemicals used widely across a variety of applications due to their durability and resistance to heat, water, and oil. However, they have been found to persist in the environment and human body for long periods of time, leading to health and environmental concerns, with various scientific studies linking certain types of PFAS to cancer. We see key regulatory milestones on the horizon this year that could prompt companies to seek PFAS alternatives, especially in consumer products. Additionally, growing mainstream media coverage of PFAS risks could lead consumers to rethink their purchasing choices, spurring companies to react. We also see the possibility that evolving litigation risk will start to impact supply chains and incentivise companies to find alternative materials. PFAS bans to impact consumer-facing products PFAS regulation in the past has focused on water pollution and bans of specific chemicals in certain use cases (e.g. PFOA bans in fire-fighting foams). We are now seeing an important shift in PFAS regulation, with an increasing prevalence of broader restrictions on PFAS usage across a wider range of sectors. records.text: he SARB sees the current policy stance as being closer to neutral rather than overly “restrictive”. The bar for further easing is surmountable, but has risen, in our view. The collapse in core-goods prices (these entered deflationary territory from October – Figure 2 overleaf) has been a big driver of the strong disinflationary trend seen in South Africa. We have long argued that this is a function of a lack of demand pressures, led by a continued moderation in unit-labour costs and a still-weak labour market which continues to crimp wage growth (see CEEMEA: Labour market key to squeeze out services CPI, dated 14 October 2025). We don’t expect these forces to meaningfully change in 2026 (see overleaf for details), but we think it’s worth exploring what a stronger recovery in domestic demand could mean for inflation. What could stronger growth mean for inflation? Our NiGEM modelled output of a 1pp positive demand shock to our GDP growth baseline for 2026 is somewhat encouraging. In such a scenario, we find that headline CPI inflation is only likely to pick up by around 25bp within 12 months compared with our current 3.2% (average) baseline forecast for 2026 (Figure 1). Given that our modelled scenario assumes an exogenised (non- reactive) monetary policy response, it suggests relatively limited risks of demand-driven inflation pressures proving a headache for the SARB in 2026. This is backed up by our assessment (overleaf) of the current composition of demand drivers. KEY MESS

records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG The UK Growth Outlook: from exogenous risks to endogenous headwinds n We expect UK GDP to slow from 1.4% in 2025 to 1.1% in 2026. External geopolitical headwinds this year, we expect, will give way to domestic headwinds. Lingering weakness in hiring, weaker pay growth, and protracted uncertainty around fiscal policy and politics will likely dampen spending and investment appetite. The good news? Policy should remain supportive. We expect both fiscal and monetary policy to help grease the wheels of the UK’s growth engine, with labour market green shoots emerging in spring. The UK growth story this year has positively surprised. Despite a softer Q3-25 GDP print, we remain cautiously optimistic on the UK economy. Indeed this past year has surprised positively on many fronts. Real GDP growth in the first half of the year accelerated to around a 2% annualised pace - supported by some front running of the trade war. Business investment was also far stronger to start the year than most expected. And yet again, we underestimated the impact of government spending - particularly public sector investment. As we enter the new year, there are still many positives. Global headwinds are slowly fading. Policy restrictiveness is slowly unwinding. Labour markets in the Euro area remain stable, with unemployment rates n expected to remain near historic lows in coming quarters. We expect wage growth to slow as real incomes stabilise, aligning with the 2% inflation target over the medium term. Core inflation has been firmer recently but is projected to dip slightly below 2% by the end of 2026, influenced by a stronger Euro and lower energy prices. Nonetheless, we see the underlying drivers of inflation—wage growth and inflation expectations—as consistent with the 2% target. Our forecasts for growth remain above the ECB’s but are slightly weaker for n inflation, supporting our expectation that rates will remain on hold in 2026. Further cuts are possible but would require a clear catalyst at this point, either via a material deterioration in the activity outlook or a more pronounced undershoot of inflation. Rate hikes would only be appropriate if significant demand-driven inflationary pressure emerged or a shock generated a large or persistent deviation of inflation from target. Kessler citizen petition is a tail risk that could be highly disruptive for ingredients: Former FDA Commissioner David Kessler submitted a citizen's petition on 6th August 2025 urging the FDA to revoke the GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) status for a wide range of refined carbohydrate ingredients—including high fructose corn syrup, dextrose, modified starches— and certain emulsifiers, citing their role in metabolic harm and chronic disease Link. In the scenario that GRAS status was revoked, we think companies would likely submit food additive registrations for the majority of products, many of which are approved in Europe. On oil, President Trump said: “We have the greatest oil companies in the world, the biggest, the greatest, and we're going to be very much involved in it.” Yet, is the country stable enough to support a meaningful rise in investments? This hinges on the governance part. On governance, President Trump said: "We can't take a chance in letting somebody else run and just take over where he left off, so we're making that decision now, we'll be involved very much.” This could eventually lead to a scenario of stability in the country. Implementation would be key, but will likely take time and involve considerable risks and unknowns. Near-term expectations of a rapid and large Venezuelan supply surge look anyway overstated, with technical limits dominating the upside. While Venezuela holds vast reserves, the absence of a stable investment climate means large-scale capex-driven growth would take years, not months. Production history underscores this constraint; output peaked at ~ 3.7 mb/d in the ‘70s, hit again a multi-year high of ~ 3.5-mb/d in ‘98, stayed above 2-m b/d in the early ‘10s, then collapsed after the 2014–15 oil price crash. From a trough below 0.3-m b/d in 2020, production has recovered to just over 1-m b/d today, nearly all exported, including via crude-for-products swaps. In terms of payback period, we believe it’s possible for AI projects in this sector to pay back in well under two years, and even within 6-12 months for targeted deployments. This is partly because many early wins are operational cost savings (which directly accrue) and partly because cloud/subscription models spread the cost rather than incurring chunky upfront capital spend. For instance, instead of buying a $1m software licence, a company might pay $100k monthly for an AI platform and might see upwards of $200k monthly savings – immediately net positive. Unilever, for example, has moved 100% of its operations to the Cloud, which is driving agility across its tech and data platforms. One must also consider ongoing costs: AI models require maintenance (model retraining, system updates). Large companies will often establish internal “AI ops” teams, which adds to payroll, and these tend to be more expensive employees, but given the 'arms race' happening in AI across the FMCG space, it is spend that is seen as necessary. SMEs might rely on vendor support or simpler auto-updating models; their ongoing cost is often just the subscription fee, which they can turn off if it stops delivering value (making it lower-risk). Fiscal Policy: PB deficits effectively tolerated, but market pressure could eventually steer Takaichi's expansionary stance in a more pragmatic direction The Takaichi administration has already passed a large supplementary budget (Figure 20) and the initial budget for FY26 is expected to reach a record high of around JPY122trn. Furthermore, management of the PB has shifted from a single-year basis to a multi-year approach, and the main gauge of fiscal sustainability has effectively changed to the government debt/GDP ratio. The key here is the “Domar condition. ” This states that as long as the nominal GDP growth rate exceeds the nominal effective interest rate (interest payments divided by the previous year’s JGB balance), the debt/GDP ratio can be maintained even if the PB is somewhat in deficit. Conversely, if the effective interest rate exceeds the GDP growth rate, a PB surplus is needed to maintain the debt/GDP ratio. Thus, relying on this logic, assuming recent circumstances remain largely unchanged, a certain PB deficit can be justified for FY26, which is convenient for the Takaichi administration in its bid to generate a “high-pressure economy” through fiscal spending. Meanwhile, Japanese investors look to have been buyers of overseas bonds and notes, adding about $1bn over the week through December 19, and purchased closer to $90bn over the full year. In the very front end, money funds had about $60bn in inflows for the week to December 30, leaving total assets at about $7.7trn, according to ICI data. That leaves money fund assets about $885bn higher over 2025, representing very strong demand despite the realized Fed rate cuts over the year. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 408/01/2026 Two key economic channels: Developments in Venezuela will have a limited direct impact on the global economy, in our view. After all, the country accounts for around 0.1% of global GDP and 0.05% of global imports. However, the latest events could affect the global economy through two key indirect channels: oil prices and geopolitical risk. In short, under our new base case and in the scenario of a strong supply increase, these channels work in opposite directions - a negative oil price shock boosts the income of oil consumers, while heightened geopolitical risk will weigh on investment and consumption, all else equal. The net impact on the global economy will depend on the magnitude, timing and persistence of each, but as Figure 4 shows, we would expect this to be generally net positive. By contrast, in scenarios in which oil supply does not increase or even contracts, we would expect, versus our base case, weaker economic activity. Modelling the shock: We use the National Institute Global Econometric Model (NiGEM) to provide a quantitative assessment of the impact of these scenarios on the global economy. We shock oil prices based on the paths outlined on page 3, while we use a popular academic measure of geopolitical risk to calibrate the change in risk premia in the model. records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Page 16 Deutsche Bank AG The Bank of England - Finding Neutral n We expect the Bank of England to deliver two further rate cuts, taking Bank Rate to our long-standing view of terminal: 3.25%. The path towards neutral will likely be clouded by enormous uncertainty - particularly given the slower wage disinflation process. The fall in headline CPI over 2026 will make the MPC's job a little easier, however. And we expect the Bank to get to neutral (~3.25%) just before summer. The risk? A slower descent as we enter the long final yards of monetary policy fine-tuning. The 2025 monetary policy story. We came into 2025 expecting four quarter-point rate cuts - taking Bank Rate from 4.75% to 3.75%. And that's likely where we will end up being with a Christmas rate cut all but certain on 18 December. While curve balls via higher payroll taxes and a surge in food inflation sparked a jump in household and business inflation expectations, genuine underlying disinflation combined with meaningful weakness in the labour market have allowed the BoE to cut Bank Rate despite the bump higher in CPI (which peaked at 3.8% y-o-y in August). In short, despite some hesitancy in November, Bank Rate cuts have followed a 'gradual and careful' direction. Policy restrictiveness has waned. records.text: January issuance technical: Headwind now, easing ahead. January is again delivering its typical seasonal lift in IG supply across the USD and EUR markets—historically one of the heaviest issuance months—while the HY seasonal is milder (Exhibit 1). The first three trading days underscore a strong start: USD IG issuance of $80 billion and EUR IG issuance of €21 billion. Conversely, USD HY issuance stands at just $6 billion while EUR HY issuance stands at zero. Within USD IG, the weekly playbook appears to be tracking history: Week 1 is usually the peak and skewed toward Yankees; Weeks 2–3 slow and tilt to financials; Week 4 is led by non‑financials (left panel, Exhibit 2). EUR IG shows a similar financials vs. non‑financials split (right panel, Exhibit 2). In our view, this implies the supply‑related technical headwind will likely peak over the coming week but should abate meaningfully by late January. The resilience of spreads suggests the pipeline was well telegraphed and absorbed. One risk to the usual late‑January lull is increased non-financial issuance, potentially related to AI, which stepped up last year and could keep prints elevated this year. AI supply analogues offer imperfect roadmaps for USD HY spread performance. Re-leveraging from debt‑funded AI capex in USD credit remains a key theme of 2026. Parliament failed to approve the entire budget before the end of last year, and some parts of the budget have therefore remained frozen under a so-called “special law” since January 1st. We expect Parliament to complete the budget negotiations over the next few months and pave the way for another small reduction in the government deficit from 5.4% of GDP to 5.1% in 2026. The approaching 2027 presidential election will likely be the dominant political theme in France this year, with incumbent President Macron unable to run again and far-right party RN currently topping polls and betting markets. As a consequence, finding a budget agreement will likely prove even more difficult this autumn, and we forecast the government deficit to remain elevated at 4.8% of GDP into 2027. Southern Europe again outperformed the rest of the Euro area notably in 2025, and investors are watching whether the economic resilience will continue (Exhibit 18). records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 05 January 2026 Citi Research 6 On the economic front, a more stable Venezuela would be positive for Colombia in the medium and long run. Before relations between the neighboring nations soured, Venezuela represented 15% of all Colombian exports. This has since fallen virtually to zero (in official figures). Regime change and return to credible democratic processes could bring back an important source of demand for agricultural goods and services. Migration flows could move in either direction depending on how fast the situation evolves, but Colombia has already received and formalized the migration situation of around 3mn Venezuelan migrants during Maduro’s regime. This suggests the shock has already been strong, and the Colombian government has been able to weather it. On the oil front, while our take overall points toward somewhat lower oil prices, Colombian oil production has fallen under President Petro, diesel remains subsidized, and a shortage of gas (broadly used for heating and cooking) is looming. Hence, a fall in energy costs is not necessarily a strong negative overall. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: decades, the outlook for long-term GDP growth will largely depend on TFP . There could be two broad categories of factors that affect TFP: 1) technological advancement, and 2) efficiency of resource allocation. Academic research has focused on worsening capital misallocation in China after the GFC due to wasteful investment and financial frictions, and the structural trend of rising services’ share of the economy could be another factor behind falling TFP growth. We believe the ongoing AI development and adoption, as well as the broader technology advancement from autonomous driving to biotech innovations, will drive labor cost savings and improve productivity, which is positive for TFP growth. However, measured labor productivity in China still falls considerably behind that of the US with current levels of exchange rates (Exhibit 24). We expect AI, when fully adopted, to raise labor productivity and boost potential GDP in China by a total of 8% cumulatively. While China’s 15th FYP focuses on technology, security, and people’s livelihood, policymakers have also pledged to further reforms aimed at building a “unified national market” (全国统一大市场) and enhancing resource allocation efficiency. In the December meeting the BoE cut rates but emphasized more caution as we approach close to neutral, with decisions on future cuts becoming a closer call. This is likely a pushback against a back-to-back cut in February. The BoE didn’t give precise guidance on the path of future cuts, but the bar is probably rising. Our view is that wage/inflation expectations should fall as we see further progress in inflation and amid a loosening labour market, allowing for gradual quarterly cuts. records.text: Over the past year, policymakers have introduced several marginal easing measures to encourage spending, including raising the minimum wage, increasing pension and healthcare benefits, subsidizing childcare, offering temporary interest subsidies for consumer loans, and expanding the supply of certain services such as elderly care, childcare and tourism. While the intention to boost domestic consumption is clear, finding effective long-term solutions requires structural reforms and takes time. Policies such as consumer goods trade-in program may only provide short-term support by pulling forward some demand from the future. To avoid sharp declines in retail sales, in late December, policymakers unveiled implementation details for the 2026 consumer goods trade-in program. Subsidy categories and levels were adjusted to maintain the program’s impact and support policy-focused areas such as people’s livelihood, security, elderly care, green products, and AI. The announced near-term funding implies full-year subsidies of approximately RMB 250 billion for the consumer goods portion of the trade-in program in 2026, slightly below the RMB 300 billion allocated in 2025. We expect full-year nominal retail sales growth to decelerate from 3.8% in 2025 to 2.7% in 2026 due to fewer overall subsidies and their fading impact. records.text: lighter benchmarks (like Brent) will be limited. In the no-relief scenario, no agreement is reached between Washington and Caracas on a way forward. Floating Venezuelan barrels and logistics would remain obstructed. Venezuelan production capacity would continue to degrade, creating some price upside versus base further down the line as well. The strong supply increase scenario, on the other hand, creates the most bearish outcome shown in Figure 3. Production would recover given structurally stronger investor involvement and better performance in critical infrastructure such as upgraders and power supply. However, given the state of the industry, the time required for new investment, and lower supplies from other sanctioned countries, we keep the price decline limited to USD5/bbl versus our base case. In the production collapse scenario, we model a full collapse of Venezuelan production, negating all current exports and obviating any growth (analogous to the production collapses we saw previously in for example Iraq and Libya), with recovery taking years. We deem this the least likely outcome but consider it important to gauge a worst-case scenario as well. We assume current production dries up completely, implying a loss of 750kbd from recent levels, without recovery in 2026 or 2027. However, with offsets from other (OPEC+) supplies and the limited impact on the sweet crude market, we believe the price impact remains limited to a USD5/bbl upside to the no-relief scenario.

We close our THOR u30-5y position at 2.05%, capturing a 24bp (USD480k) profit on the trade. We take profit on our THOR u30-5y payer trade idea (see EM rates: Add THB 5y5y payer, dated 15 September) as we have reached our target, capturing 29bp (USD580k) on the trade. We initiated this trade after Thailand's new prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, formed a cabinet of experienced technocrats and signaled reviving economic growth as his top priority. The interest rate curve had bull flattened significantly in the months prior to our trade entry, and we anticipated a potential sell-off in the long end. Our view has largely played out, with the government implementing measures, such as cash handouts and debt resolution programs to support the economy. Tourism has also picked up in Q4, which was supportive for the economy. Although the Bank of Thailand (BoT) cut its policy rate to 1.25% in December, this was in line with market expectations. Most recently, the BoT has continued to stress limited space for further easing, contributing to a further selloff in rates. Given the trade has reached our target, we close our THOR u30-5y position at 2.10%, capturing a 29bp (USD580k) profit on the trade. We will look to reassess and potentially reenter after the elections.

records.text: What if the Street revalues Church & Dwight's architected organic sales? Lauren R. Lieberman BCI, US It is no secret that M&A has been central to Church & Dwight’s strategy, and we’ve long believed valuation is steep in this context. M&A, as we see it, is the core tenet of Church & Dwight’s strategy, with the company having acquired 26 brands since 2004, and seven of eight “power brands” have joined the stable via M&A. Church & Dwight has been clear about its priorities, citing acquisitions as the highest value use of free cash flow. In fact, we recall CHD overtly describing itself as an “acquisition platform” in the mid-2010s, though similar “platform” language existed far before then (such as in Feb '07, the company noted, "We have a very strong platform of both household and personal care and the ability to integrate other CPG brands into it very effectively"). While this nomenclature has since exited the lexicon (last cited in 2019), nothing has changed with regard to corporate strategy, and the company has said its approach to M&A is “category agnostic” within the confines of key criteria – #1 or #2 brand, high- growth/margin, and asset light. In this context, despite CHD’s strong balance sheet and healthy dollar-based earnings growth, we’ve long argued that Church & Dwight’s elevated multiple is not warranted, with shares having traded at a +35% premium to Large-Cap Staples on average over the past 5 years, even though its growth model is primarily acquisition led. records.text: s likely to remain cautious about conducting traditional, high-profile easing measures, such as policy rate or RRR cuts, and rely more on flexible liquidity operations. Therefore, we expect only a dual cut (a 50bp RRR cut and a 10bp policy rate cut) in Q1 and another 10bp policy rate cut in Q3, despite the still-weak domestic demand and potentially large government bond issuance in 2026 (Exhibit 18). Loan growth slowed markedly in 2025, reflecting softening loan demand from the real economy. By contrast, total social financing (TSF) stock growth temporarily picked up to 9% yoy in July, driven by record-high government bond issuance. The PBOC has continued to downplay loan growth as a leading indicator of economic activity, while placing more emphasis on targeted credit policy support to technology, green economy, small businesses, elderly care, and digital economy. This suggests the PBOC is willing to tolerate further moderation in loan growth. Looking ahead, TSF stock growth is likely to continue to outperform loan growth in 2026. We expect TSF stock growth to rise modestly to 8.8% in 2026 from 8.5% expected in 2025, as continued fiscal expansion is likely to more than offset the drag from the still-weak loan demand. That said, Treasury's T-bill net issuance needs will be quite hefty at over $700bn before accounting for Fed purchases if they leave coupon auction sizes unchanged for all of this year. That said, there is considerable uncertainty around several aspects of this forecast. The FOMC has not committed to any level of T-bill demand this year and has delegated its monthly decision-making on the size of these purchases directly to the Desk at the New York Fed. Moreover, the December meeting minutes show a lack of consensus around the framework for how to structure RMPs, which we think makes the magnitude of Fed purchases after Q1 a bit more uncertain, and there is a risk they are quite a bit lower than in our baseline. In addition, there are other upside risks to T-bill supply for this year, including potential IEEPA tariff refunds and fiscal stimulus ahead of midterms. records.text: What if the dining-out to dining-in trend continues in the UK? Matthew Clements Barclays, UK UK consumers are dining out less and dining in more, driven primarily by pressure on disposable incomes and high price inflation at restaurants. M&S, Tesco and Sainsbury are the natural beneficiaries of this trend, given their established positioning in premium own-label, supporting market share performance and margin development. We expect this trend to continue in 2026 and potentially beyond, driven by cost pressures impacting the restaurant industry, pressure on household disposable income, increased GLP-1 usage, consumer focus on health, and continued innovation by the grocers. A shift from dining-out to dining-in has benefited UK supermarkets UK consumers have been switching from dining-out to dining-in, reducing the 'share of stomach' spent at restaurants to the benefit of supermarkets. • The pandemic instigated a dramatic change in consumption habits, but the dining-out share of household expenditure on food has not recovered to pre-pandemic levels since the re- opening. Part of this can likely be explained by habitual eating-at-home after lock-downs and continued working from home. Discretionary spending came under pressure during the cost- of-living crisis of 2022-23, while high energy prices and minimum wage increases squeezed restaurateurs. • Restaurants were disproportionately impacted by the cost pressures resulting from the Autumn 2024 Budget. records.text: 5 January 2026 UK economic notes Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG The fiscal headroom. The Chancellor took a big step to remedy her wafer thin buffers in the Autumn Budget. And while the main primary headroom has more than doubled (GBP 22bn), it still remains historically low. Indeed, a good rule of thumb in our view is to maintain something closer to a 1% of GDP fiscal buffer to avoid unnecessary volatility in day-to-day policy making. As the OBR itself notes, soft changes in projections can easily wipe away the Chancellor's headroom, from say a further downgrade to productivity to current levels, i.e. ~0.5%. This would leave the current budget deficit in negative territory all through the forecast horizon. Other small changes can have a meaningful impact too. A 0.1pp reduction in nominal GDP in each year of the OBR forecast horizon could knock off GBP 14bn from the current budget surplus in 2029/30. A 1pp increase in gilt yields and Bank Rate expectations would reduce the current balance by GBP 16bn in 2029/30. A 1pp rise in RPI across the forecast horizon could pull the current balance down by GBP 10bn in 2029/30. An an AI/equity correction could also pose risks to the public finances, with a global correction (implying around a 35% fall in UK and world equity prices) could see the current budget surplus narrowed to only GBP 6bn. The rollout of “anti-involution” policies since July has drawn comparisons with the supply side reform in 2016-18, prompting market speculation over when PPI inflation and changes in GDP deflator might turn positive. These expectations have been reinforced by the acceleration in M1 growth, which historically tended to precede reflation by around 12 months. Meanwhile, the recent uptick in core CPI inflation has raised questions over whether headline CPI inflation could rebound to and stabilize above 1% yoy in the coming months. In our view, the reflation process is likely to remain gradual. We expect year-over-year PPI inflation to turn positive in early 2027, while headline CPI inflation should largely remain below 1% in 2026, despite temporary support to core inflation from the sharp rise in gold prices and the consumer trade-in program. records.text: 5 January 2026 Hsueh On Oil Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Short term supply downside Venezuelan oil production has been under pressure since the announcement of a US 'total and complete' blockade of sanctioned oil vessels on 16 December. One key question is whether this US blockade remains in place. If it does, then Venezuela is vulnerable to supply downside. Exports of crude oil have reportedly been reduced to zero as of early January, owing to the US blockade, and PDVSA has begun cutting production as a result of insufficient storage capacity. Additionally, imports of diluent have been disrupted, and these are needed to maintain production and transport of heavy crude oil2 . According to Reuters, these shipments have been disrupted because Russia uses sanctioned vessels to deliver its naphtha cargoes.3 The answer to the question may depend on the nature of the US relationship with the acting president of Venezuela, Delcy Rodriguez, who has called for a "balanced and respectful" international relationship, and extended an invitation to the US government to work on a cooperation agenda.4 The outcome of this relationship will help determine whether the US may eventually see fit to lift sanctions on Venezuela. The second half of 2025 represented the bottoming process for key macro gauges, and we see 2026 as a year of re-acceleration in these indicators. Exhibit 1 shows that the 45-month cycle amplitude of the ISM Manufacturing PMI points to a rebound. This "scheduled" recovery was delayed by Liberation Day, but not cancelled, in our view. Further supporting this stance is Exhibit 2 , which illustrates that the recovery we saw in earnings revisions breadth (which has another leg higher to go, in our view) also points to a rebound in the ISM. Exhibit 3 is a new chart from us, which shows a fairly strong inverse relationship over time between rates and the ISM. Note the extended lag in this relationship—i.e., it takes ~18 months for lower yields in rate of change terms to flow through to business activity. records.text: Growing awareness could trigger changes in consumer behaviour Crucially, we think demand for PFAS solutions could accelerate ahead of regulation if consumer awareness grows and leads to purchasing behaviours that prioritise avoiding PFAS, incentivising companies to expand PFAS-free product offerings. Evidence of growing consumer awareness is reflected in Figure 77 which indicates a rising number of Google searches for PFAS. A survey of UK consumers by YouGov showed that six in ten were willing to accept a reduction in performance or an increase in cost for products that didn't contain PFAS. Public awareness in the UK remained low, though, with only ~30% having already heard of PFAS, indicating there is still a lot of potential for awareness to grow further. We think more brands labelling products as "PFAS-free" , especially in apparel and cookware, and further mainstream media coverage of PFAS-related health risks (such as the recent BBC Panorama documentary about PFAS) will help educate more consumers and amplify demand for safer alternatives. Looking ahead, we expect nominal export growth to remain solid at 5.6% in 2026 (vs. 5.5% in 2025) in USD terms (Exhibit 5). The housing market may remain a key consideration in H1, while the weight given to growth could rise towards H2, in our view. 2025 in review: This paper follows up on the policy rate pathway research for 2025, published in January last year, in which we set out how we saw three key variables (inflation, growth and financial stability) changing over time, and their potential effect on rate decisions (see Bank of Korea: Policy rate pathway for 2025). Looking back at 2025, the BoK delivered two 25bp rate cuts in H1 to support economic recovery, but then shifted to keep rates on hold in H2. That surprised markets which had expected an extension of the rate-cutting cycle, and reflected the BoK placing greater weight on its concerns around financial stability (see Bank of Korea: Hawkish tone suggests an extended rate hold, dated 27 November 2025). The CBC continued to keep rates on hold in 2025, as growth surged above potential amid stable inflation, alongside lingering concerns around the housing market (see Taiwan: Policy in a good place, with dovish rhetoric, dated 19 December 2025). records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 05 January 2026 Citi Research 2 Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro was captured by US military forces on the morning of January 3rd. Maduro and his wife have been indicted on drug trafficking charges in the US – along with Venezuelan Minister of the Interior, Diosdado Cabello – and will be subsequently tried. Maduro's arrest and extradition to the US sets a new chapter for Venezuela and may have some spillover on Latam and general EM risk. We see potential for future easing in oil prices – not strong enough to generate a price shock in EM energy credits, but positive for short-term energy inflation paths. We have a bias to buy any risk spike generated by this geopolitical event. US President Donald Trump has said the US administration will “run the country” in the meantime. Focus on the oil sector will remain a key driver of conversations, with the Trump administration interested in protecting US firms in an infrastructure build-up in Venezuela. Delcy Rodriguez, VP, has been sworn in as acting president. The selection of Delcy Rodríguez to lead the interim governing framework suggests a controlled recalibration rather than a disruptive break with the past. While signs are in place to begin a rebuild, we note caution around continued screwworm infections in Mexican cattle, a key feeder to Southern US farms, that could disrupt or delay a full industry recovery. Rebuild signs are in place While the US herd count remained muted in the 2025 January and July cattle inventory updates, we see that signs for a turnaround are now in place. The July 1 USDA cattle figures, while still near all-time lows, posted an overall headcount of 94.2mn that was better than the market expectation of 93.6mn.
